sens: Interrogative word to ask for identification or description
Interrogative adverb to ask for the cause or reason
Interrogative adverb to ask about time, duration, or moment
Indefinite pronoun: something, anything
H4100.detail:
1. "What" inquires about the nature or identity of something. In Genesis 2:19, God brings the animals to man "to see what he would call them": Adam must identify and name each creature. This is the most direct use of the word.

2. "Why" asks for the reason or cause of an action. In 2 Chronicles 25:19, one king reproaches another: "Why engage in a foolish enterprise?" He questions the motive behind a decision. This meaning is very common in biblical dialogues.

3. "When" or "until when" inquires about time or duration. In Psalms 74:9, the psalmist cries: "no one among us knows how long..." — he asks how long God's silence will last. This temporal nuance appears frequently.

4. In an indefinite context, the word designates "something" or "anything," without inquiry. In Jeremiah 6:20, God asks: "What need have I of incense?" — not to ask for information, but to deny the usefulness of what is offered.
H4100.origine: This Hebrew root word comes from the family of Semitic interrogatives, which is very ancient and fundamental. It was used to inquire about quality, nature, or time. Its flexibility — able to carry different prepositions to ask "by what?", "until when?", "why?" — makes it a very adaptable tool in biblical conversation. The word is omnipresent in the dialogues of the Old Testament.
H4100.emploi: This word appears 659 times in the Hebrew Bible, making it one of the most frequent. It arises wherever conversation becomes lively: direct questions ("What have you done?"), objections ("Why have you deceived me?"), doubts ("How can I know this?"). It structures the dialogues of Genesis, the laments of the Psalms, the exhortations of the prophets. Its multiple translations in French — "what", "why", "when", "which", "what", "how" — show that Hebrew concentrates in a single word inquiries that we must distinguish. Its context always determines the exact meaning.
H4100.portee: This small word reveals the very nature of biblical religious life: an ongoing dialogue between man and God. The questions it introduces are never trivial — they touch on identity ("who are you?"), legitimacy ("why?"), time ("when?"). Reading this word invites us to ask ourselves the real questions: about the meaning of life, about God, about the future. God's silence in the face of our questions becomes as eloquent as His answers.

sens: Direct inquiry: "what?"
That which, the thing that (relative)
Any, everything that (indefinite)
How?, why? (with preposition)
H4101.detail:
1. The word poses a simple and direct question: "what?", "what is it?" — the most elementary question. In Daniel 2:15, Arjoc asks the king, "Why is the decree so severe?", using this word to seek an explanation for a decision.
2. It can also designate "that which" or "the thing that", as a relative: what you deem good (Ezra 7:18) — that is, "the thing you judge to be good".
3. It functions as an indefinite: "anything, everything that". The necessary things (Ezra 6:9) — that is, what is required, necessary — shows this meaning.
4. Placed after a preposition ("of what", "for what"), it introduces a question or a cause: "for fear that evil may increase" (Ezra 4:22) — literally "for fear that what, an evil...".
H4101.origine: This is the simplest and oldest Hebrew word for asking "what?". It comes from a very ancient root shared by many Semitic languages. It is a fundamental interrogative particle, with no special grammatical link: it survives as is in biblical Aramaic (the language of Daniel and Ezra), where it functions exactly the same way.
H4101.emploi: This word appears 11 times, almost exclusively in the Aramaic portions of Daniel (9 occurrences) and the book of Ezra (4 occurrences). In Daniel 2, it dominates the questions of Nebuchadnezzar and his wise men: "what, why, that which". It serves to pose a question ("Why is the decree so severe?"), to express uncertainty ("that which is in darkness"), and to construct relatives and indefinites. It is a very flexible word, changing meaning according to the context and the preposition that precedes it.
H4101.portee: This small word reminds us that the Bible provides answers to the simplest and most urgent questions of man: "what?", "why?". Nebuchadnezzar, the powerful king, asks questions, and Daniel answers by revealing what is hidden. Biblical faith does not invite us to silence our questions, but to pose them to God and listen for His answer.

sens: To wait slowly, to drag one's feet before acting
To remain in place without leaving
To defer, to postpone
To hesitate or be paralyzed by astonishment
H4102.detail:
1. This verb describes the action of not hurrying, dragging one's feet before doing something. Lot "lingered" to leave Sodom before its destruction, as if he hesitated or had difficulty deciding (Genesis 19:16). It is a slowness of execution that wastes precious time.
2. The verb can also simply mean to stay, to remain in place. In Judges 19:8, the father-in-law invites the Levite to "stay" until evening to eat together — it is not hesitation, but prolonging a stay.
3. In some contexts, it expresses the idea of postponing, making wait. Joseph's brothers say: "If we had not delayed", meaning if we had not dragged our feet (Genesis 43:10).
4. Rarely, the verb can express astonishment or confusion of mind, as in Isaiah 29:9 where the people are "astonished" — paralyzed by shock.
H4102.origine: The root מהה (mahah) evokes an idea of slow movement or pause. It belongs to a small group of Hebrew verbs expressing hesitation and delay. The fundamental meaning is that of something stretching out in time, taking time to occur or to be completed.
H4102.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Old Testament. It is concentrated in the narratives of the Pentateuch and Judges (Genesis, Exodus, Judges), then sporadically in poetic or prophetic texts. In Genesis 19:16 and 43:10, it denotes slowness or hesitation to act. In Exodus 12:39, it emphasizes the urgency of the Exodus: the Hebrews could not "delay". In Judges 3:26, Ehud takes "flight" while his pursuers delay. The nuance is therefore flexible: hesitation, involuntary delay, prolonged stay, or interruption of action due to astonishment.
H4102.portee: This word reminds us that decisive moments do not tolerate procrastination. Lot who "lingered" risked perishing with Sodom; the Israelites would have been caught if they had delayed in the Exodus. For the believer, it invites recognition of when God calls to act without delay, and not to let hesitation or fear paralyze us in obedience.

sens: Confused and noisy agitation, general disorder
Panic, fear, dismay in the face of a threat
Chaotic military destruction or defeat
Internal state of anxiety, discomfort
H4103.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a noise of confusion, a sonic and physical chaos: in 1 Samuel 14:20, after God threw panic among the Philistines, "the confusion was extreme" — they fought against each other in complete disorder.
2. It expresses the terror and fear that grips a city or a people in the face of danger. In 1 Samuel 5:9, when the ark of God arrives in Ashdod, the hand of the Lord strikes the city and there is a "very great dismay" — the people panic, seized by fear.
3. It is also the military effect of defeat: in Deuteronomy 7:23, God promises to put the enemies of Israel "completely to rout," meaning to strike them with chaos and confusion in battle, leading to their destruction.
4. The word can describe an internal state: in Proverbs 15:16, "a little with the fear of the Lord" is better "than great treasure with trouble" — here, it refers to the anxiety and discomfort that oppress the soul.
H4103.origine: The Hebrew word מְהוּמָה (mehumah) comes from a root expressing tumultuous and confused movement. It belongs to a family of words in Hebrew that all evoke disorder: noise, confusion, agitation. It is a word that paints a chaotic state — not a state of calm organization, but of complete disarray.
H4103.emploi: This word appears 12 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the historical and prophetic books. It often describes God's intervention: either to terrify the enemies of Israel and put them to flight (Deuteronomy 7:23, 1 Samuel 14:20, Zechariah 14:13), or to strike a city with a plague that causes panic (1 Samuel 5:9, 5:11). In the prophets, it denounces the moral and social chaos that reigns due to sin: Ezekiel 22:5 speaks of the "confusion" of Jerusalem, Amos 3:9 denounces the "confusion" in Samaria. In Proverbs 15:16, the word changes meaning: it is no longer an external phenomenon, but an internal condition — the trouble of one who lacks the peace of God.
H4103.portee: This word shows how God controls history: He can transform a powerful enemy into chaotic and panicked confusion, or conversely strike a city with terror to warn it. For the believing reader, this teaches that the true peril is not having little, but living without the peace of God — internal trouble is to be feared more than external poverty (Proverbs 15:16). It is a call to seek first the fear of the Lord, the source of true rest.

sens: Eunuch in the service of King Ahasuerus
H4104.detail: Mehuman is one of the seven eunuchs who served King Ahasuerus at the Persian royal court. His name appears only once in the Bible, in the list of eunuchs appointed by the king on the seventh day of a great banquet, when the king's heart was merry with wine (Esther 1:10).
H4104.origine: The name Mehuman means "faithful" or "one who remains faithful" in Hebrew. It is a Semitic compound name that reflects the qualities expected of a trusted servant of the king. This type of name was common among royal Persian servants during the time of the Exile and Return.
H4104.emploi: Mehuman is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Esther 1:10, as the first of the seven eunuchs named who served before King Ahasuerus. These eunuchs formed a group of high servants responsible for the king's personal service. Their presence in this account underscores the administrative organization and protocol of the Persian royal court during the Exile.

sens: Woman of the patriarchal era, wife of King Hadad of Edom
Mother of Shemaiah, the false prophet opposed to Nehemiah
H4105G.detail:
1. Mehéthabeel is the wife of King Hadad of Edom, mentioned in the genealogical lists of the kings of Edom. She is the daughter of Mathred and Mezahab (Genesis 36:39 and 1 Chronicles 1:50). Her name appears in the historical records of the Old Testament as part of the royal lineages of that region.

2. Another character of the same name (or from her lineage) is the ancestor of Shemaiah, a false prophet hired by Tobiah and Sanballat to oppose Nehemiah during the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem. This mention shows how an ancient name reappears in the later history of the people of Israel.
H4105G.origine: The name Mehéthabeel means "favorite of God" or "God has favored." It is composed of the idea of divine favor and the acknowledgment of the divine name. In Hebrew, this name expresses a blessing or a mark of divine favor toward the person who bears it. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains a reference to God.
H4105G.emploi: Mehéthabeel is mentioned twice in the Segond, both in genealogical contexts. First, in Genesis 36:39, she is identified as the wife of King Hadad of Edom and daughter of Mathred, in the list of kings of Edom before the Israelite monarchy. Secondly, in 1 Chronicles 1:50, the same fact is recalled in the parallel genealogy of the kings of Edom. Another Mehéthabeel is mentioned indirectly as the ancestor of the false prophet Shemaiah during Nehemiah's time, although the latter does not appear in the key verses.
H4105G.portee: The name Mehéthabeel, meaning "favorite of God," reminds us that even the wives of foreign kings and the ancestors of Israel's adversaries bore names expressing divine blessing. This shows the universality of faith in God beyond the borders of Israel and invites us to consider how God cares for all peoples.

sens: Man of the Exile and Return period, ancestor of the false prophet Shemaiah
H4105H.detail: Mehétabeel is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the Exile and Return in Judah. He is the ancestor of the false prophet Shemaiah, father of Delajah (Nehemiah 6:10). Shemaiah, his descendant, was a straw man hired by Tobiah and Sanballat to trap Nehemiah by pushing him to commit sacrilege in the Temple.
H4105H.origine: The name means "favorite of God" or "beloved of God" in Hebrew. It is composed of the idea of divine favor. In the Old Testament, this name is also borne by the daughter of Matred, wife of King Hadad of Edom, but this is not the same person mentioned in Nehemiah.
H4105H.emploi: Mehétabeel is cited only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 6:10. He is named as the grandfather of the false prophet Shemaiah, who lived during the return from exile under Nehemiah. The context shows that Shemaiah had been hired by Nehemiah's enemies (Tobiah and Sanballat) to intimidate and deceive him. His name recalls a respectable ancestor, perhaps to lend credibility to this false prophet.
H4105H.portee: This character illustrates how the enemies of God's people use deception and respectable appearances to hinder the divine work. The name of a honorable ancestor does not guarantee the integrity of descendants: Shemaiah, despite his heritage, sold himself to those who wished harm to Nehemiah.

sens: Who is quick in their gestures or actions
Who has competence and know-how in an art or trade
Who acts with promptness and diligence
Who shows zeal and eagerness
H4106.detail:
1. Skilled first describes the speed of execution: one who does things quickly, without dragging. It is the image of work well done, of a hand that does not linger (Psalms 45:2: the pen of the skilled writer runs across the paper).

2. The word then broadens to competence: one who is quick is so because they know their trade. This is why skilled designates the artisan or scribe mastering their art. Ezra 7:6 states explicitly: Ezra was well-versed in the law of Moses, meaning he knew it so well that he could explain and transmit it without hesitation.

3. Skill also manifests through diligence: one who acts with eagerness and zeal, who fully commits to what they do. Isaiah 16:5 speaks of a zealous judge for justice, meaning attentive and diligent.

4. Finally, the word denotes visible excellence: the skilled man in his work stands out and earns respect. Proverbs 22:29 illustrates this well: one who excels in their work is noticed by kings, while the mediocre remains in obscurity.
H4106.origine: The Hebrew word מָהִיר comes from a root expressing speed and promptness. This root evokes the idea of a brief, effective action that does not linger. Skill is thus primarily thought of as agility: that of the musician's finger, the sculptor's chisel, the scribe's hand. From there, the word enriches: to be quick in a gesture is to be expert; to be expert is to show zeal.
H4106.emploi: The word appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of professional or moral excellence. Ezra 7:6 applies it to a scribe competent in law; Psalms 45:2 puts it in the mouth of a poet speaking of a gifted writer; Proverbs 22:29 recommends it as a path to social success; Isaiah 16:5 attributes it to a conscientious judge. The word thus values the person who masters their field and fully commits to it, whether they are literate, an artist, or a magistrate.
H4106.portee: This word reminds the believer that competence and diligence are gifts to be honored. Ezra, the skilled scribe, becomes an instrument in God's hand to restore the people. Proverbs affirms it: professional excellence opens doors. It is a call to develop our talents without laziness, to put them at the service of what God asks, as Ezra well-versed in the Law does for his people.

sens: Reduce the purity of a liquid by adding water or another substance
Weaken, diminish the strength or quality of something
H4107.detail:
1. The word first describes the concrete action of mixing liquid with water to reduce its concentration: in Isaiah 1:22, the wine "cut" with water is diluted wine, weakened, of lesser quality.
2. Figuratively, it means to weaken or degrade something immaterial — a value, a quality, a promise — by compromising it or making it less pure. The prophet uses the image of mixed wine to denounce moral compromise: everything has degraded, even what should be precious and pure.
H4107.origine: This Hebrew verb expresses the idea of a gradual reduction: to cut, to reduce, to take away. The basic image is that of amputation or decrease. When one dilutes wine, they "cut" its strength. The word can also evoke the idea of circumcision — a ritual cutting — which reinforces the idea of modification, separation, or reduction of an original integrity.
H4107.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 1:22. The prophet uses it to describe wine weakened by water: an image of Israel's moral decline. Everything that should be pure and authentic — silver, wine, justice, faithfulness — has proven counterfeit or degraded. The context shows a corrupt society where nothing true can be found.
H4107.portee: This word speaks to us about the danger of gradual compromise: we can weaken our integrity, our faithfulness, or our faith by accepting "mixtures" that seem minor. Like Israel, we risk presenting ourselves before God with something degraded instead of the pure heart He desires. It is a call to remain authentic and whole in our commitment to Him.

sens: Action of walking, moving on foot
Distance covered while walking, duration of a day's walk
Path, passage, alley
Access, freedom to move or go back and forth
H4109.detail:
1. The word first designates the simple act of walking, the act of moving forward. It is the physical action of putting one foot in front of the other (Zechariah 3:7: "If you walk in my ways").
2. It also means the distance covered while walking, especially when talking about a whole day: Nineveh was "three days' walk" from Jonah's starting point (Jonah 3:3), meaning it took three days on foot to cross it. Jonah covers "a day's walk" before he begins to preach (Jonah 3:4).
3. The word also designates a space intended for circulation, an alley or a way: in front of the temple chambers stretched "a wide alley of ten cubits" (Ezekiel 42:4).
4. Finally, it can mean access or permission to move freely: Zechariah promises the priest that he will have "free access among those who are here" (Zechariah 3:7), meaning he will be able to move without hindrance.
H4109.origine: This word comes from the Hebrew root halakh, which means "to go, to walk." Mahalhakh is the nominal form that designates the action or result of this walk. The same root is found in other biblical words, such as mahlek ("path"). It is a very concrete image: that of the body's movement from one place to another.
H4109.emploi: The word appears five times in the Old Testament, mainly in narratives and descriptions of the temple. Nehemiah uses it to talk about the duration of the journey he must take when leaving the king of Persia (Nehemiah 2:6). Ezekiel uses it to describe the spaces and passages of the temple building (Ezekiel 42:4). Jonah uses it twice to express the greatness of Nineveh and his own progress in the city (Jonah 3:3-4). Zechariah uses it figuratively to signify access to worship (Zechariah 3:7). The word can thus be very concrete or become more abstract when it comes to freedom or favor.
H4109.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, the path and the walk are never insignificant details. When the word of God invites to "walk in His ways" (Zechariah 3:7), it invites to a movement that is not only physical: it is obedience, following, faithfulness. The word also teaches us that access to God is not automatic: it is a favor, a permission granted to one who observes divine orders.

sens: The glory, the honor one acquires through one's actions
That for which one is known, reputed among men
H4110.detail:
1. Renown is the glory or honor that a person builds through their actions and conduct. It is what makes people talk about them, for better or for worse. In Proverbs 27:21, the text compares a man to a furnace that purifies metal: just as gold is tested and refined in fire, a man is known and judged by what he reveals about himself — his renown, that is, the reputation he has built.
2. It is also what defines one in the eyes of others: the name one carries in the community, what one leaves as a mark. Renown can be good or bad depending on our choices; it is the fruit of who we truly are.
H4110.origine: The Hebrew word māhaləl comes from a root that means "to praise," "to celebrate." Renown is thus etymologically what is praised, celebrated, or spoken of — the noise made around someone. It is the public culmination of a life: one is renowned when one is talked about, praised, or blamed.
H4110.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 27:21. It is used in a context of judgment and character: renown becomes the test of what one truly is, just as a furnace tests gold. It is a term of wisdom, inviting reflection on the lasting impact of our actions on our reputation.
H4110.portee: This verse reminds us that our actions shape our renown — what others and we ourselves know about us. For the Christian, this invites a life of integrity: our choices gradually build the reputation we leave behind. It is a call not to live for the glory of men, but to cultivate a reputation of faithfulness and righteousness.

sens: Man of the generation before the Flood
Son of Kenan and father of Jared
Fourth descendant of Adam through the line of Seth
H4111G.detail:
1. Mahalaleel is a pre-flood patriarch, meaning a man who lived before the Flood described in Genesis 6-7. He belongs to the long chain of generations that God preserved before purifying the earth with water.
2. In the genealogy given in Genesis 5, Mahalaleel is the son of Kenan and the father of Jared (Genesis 5:12-15). His name appears in this regular succession where each father lists his son and the age at which he fathered him.
3. According to the numbers in the account, Mahalaleel lived a total of 895 years (Genesis 5:17), which is characteristic of the extraordinarily long lives of the pre-flood people. After the birth of Jared, he lived another 830 years and had other children.
H4111G.origine: The name Mahalaleel comes from Hebrew and means "praise of God" or "God praised": it is composed of "mahol" (praise, glory) and "El" (God). This name reflects the piety of that pre-flood period, when men still recognized the presence and majesty of God. It is also mentioned in the genealogy of Luke 3:37 (spelled Malaleleel in Greek), in the genealogical line of Jesus according to the Gospel of Luke.
H4111G.emploi: Mahalaleel appears six times in the Bible, always in genealogical contexts. Four occurrences are found in Genesis 5:12-17, where he is presented in the order of generations from Adam to Noah. His name also appears in 1 Chronicles 1:2, which reproduces the same genealogy. He represents an essential link in the divine heritage chain before the Flood, a witness of the time when God still visibly walked with men.
H4111G.portee: Mahalaleel reminds us that God preserved a faithful lineage before the judgment of the Flood. His long name, "praise of God," suggests that in this ancient world, the memory of God and His worship were not forgotten. His existence proves that the revelation of God dates back to the origins of humanity, long before the Law was given to Moses.

sens: man of Judah returned from exile
father of Shephatiah
H4111H.detail: Mahalaleel is a man from the tribe of Judah who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile, probably during the time of Nehemiah. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:4, where he appears in the genealogy of the sons of Judah who resettled in the capital: he is an ancestor of Shephatiah. His name means "praise of God" in Hebrew, reflecting the piety of the families of Judah who returned to rebuild Jerusalem.
H4111H.origine: The name Mahalaleel means "praise of God": it combines two Hebrew roots expressing the idea of praising and glorifying. This name was borne by figures in the Old Testament at different times: an antediluvian ancestor in the line of Seth (the fourth descendant of Adam according to Genesis 5), and this Mahalaleel from the time of exile and return, a descendant of Perez son of Judah.
H4111H.emploi: Mahalaleel appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:4. He is a man of Judah who is listed among the inhabitants of Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is presented as the father of Shephatiah, which shows his role in the restoration of the Jewish community in Jerusalem. His inclusion in this genealogy indicates that he came from a recognized and established family in the holy city.

sens: to strike someone with force
corporal punishment, physical punishment
painful consequence of a foolish action
H4112.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of striking someone with force, a physical shock. In Proverbs 18:6, the fool by his words "provokes blows": his quarrels and insolence attract violent reactions against him.
2. It also means corporal punishment or physical punishment inflicted. Proverbs 19:29 speaks of the "blows" ready for the backs of fools: it is the correction deserved by one who mocks.
3. In a broader sense, it refers to any painful or unfortunate consequence that strikes one who acts wrongly: the fool receives the "blow" of the return of his actions.
H4112.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to strike" or "to beat." It is a noun formed to designate the result, the effect of this action: the blow itself. The root evokes the physical, rapid, and painful impact.
H4112.emploi: The word appears twice in the book of Proverbs, in chapters 18 and 19. In both cases, it concerns punishments or negative consequences that strike one who acts wrongly: the fool who provokes quarrels, the mocker who insults. It is always in a context of natural justice: one who sins through their words or attitude receives "blows" in return. The repetition in a small space shows that it is an important lesson of the book of Proverbs.
H4112.portee: This word reminds us of the biblical reality that actions have consequences: our foolish words and pride can expose us to painful reactions. It is a call to wisdom: to measure our words and attitude to avoid the "blow" of return. Behind this simple image lies a profound lesson about personal responsibility and the justice of God.

sens: Deep pit filled with water
Bottomless pit, place of fall and perdition
H4113.detail:
1. The word literally designates a pit or a deep cavity filled with water — the image of a well or a dark depth from which one cannot escape. In Psalms 140:11, the psalmist wishes that his persecutors be hurled into these abysses, from which they cannot rise: it is a place of definitive destruction.
2. By extension, the abyss becomes the image of the pit of perdition, of irreversible disaster. It is a symbol of fall, annihilation, or divine judgment — the place where the enemies of God or those who turn away from Him disappear.
H4113.origine: The Hebrew word מַהֲמֹרָה (maharah) is formed from a root expressing the idea of hollow or depth. The image is that of a stagnant water pit or a bottomless well — a cavernous space where water accumulates in darkness. This root also appears in other words designating depths or cavities, and it evokes the idea of what is unfathomable and inaccessible.
H4113.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 140:11, where it describes the fate wished for the wicked. In this context of a prayer for vengeance, the abyss is presented as a punishment: it is the place where God hurls those who plot evil and persecute the righteous. This type of imagery — falling into a deep pit — is common in the psalms to express complete ruin or divine judgment.
H4113.portee: This word reminds the reader that evil has consequences: God does not leave malice and persecution unpunished. The abyss symbolizes total rupture with God and the impossibility of turning back — it is an invitation not to harden oneself against God. For the believer, it is also an assurance that God takes care to protect those who trust in Him from the malice of others.

sens: Violent overthrow of a city or country
Divine catastrophe, complete annihilation
Total ruin and devastation
H4114.detail:
1. The word designates the violent overthrow and physical destruction of a city or an entire territory. It is the image of a city completely ravaged, whose inhabitants are scattered or killed and from which nothing remains. In Isaiah 1:7, the prophet speaks of strangers who "devastate and destroy" the land of Israel, with the same violence inflicted on the Canaanite cities.
2. The Bible uses this word specifically to refer to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, caused by God's own judgment. It is not an ordinary ruin, but a supernatural catastrophe: God "destroyed" these cursed cities, erasing all trace of habitation. This judgment becomes in Scripture the model of what it means to be annihilated by God (Jeremiah 49:18; Amos 4:11).
3. By extension, the word describes any total and irreversible annihilation. The prophets apply it to Babylon (Isaiah 13:19) and Edom (Jeremiah 50:40), announcing that these powerful empires will meet the same end as the cities of the Jordan: no man will dwell there anymore, silence and desolation will reign forever.
H4114.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to overthrow, to turn back." The starting image is that of a city being overturned, turned upside down. In biblical Hebrew, this noun is almost always used to speak of the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, which shows how much this divine judgment has marked Israel's memory as the ultimate symbol of God's wrath.
H4114.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the prophets. It is first used to literally describe the historical destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Deuteronomy 29:23; Jeremiah 49:18; Jeremiah 50:40; Amos 4:11), which God "destroyed" in His anger. The prophets then use it to announce that enemy nations will meet the same fate: Babylon and Edom will be "destroyed" like those cursed cities (Isaiah 13:19; Jeremiah 50:40). In a single passage (Isaiah 1:7), the word applies to the devastation of Israel itself, showing that Israel risks suffering the same destruction as the cities of judgment if the people do not repent.
H4114.portee: This word reminds the reader that God judges sin with absolute severity. The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah is not a forgotten event: it becomes a living warning, the seal of divine wrath on immorality and rebellion. At the same time, the prophets use this word to promise that the enemies of God's people will suffer this judgment, and to warn Israel itself of the risk it runs. It is a word of justice that should lead the people to repentance.

sens: Instrument of physical punishment that immobilizes the body in an uncomfortable position
Place of detention where prisoners are held
H4115.detail:
1. The word first designates an instrument of torture or punishment that forces the body to take a contorted and painful posture — somewhat like stocks or chains that twist the limbs. It is a device of physical suffering: Jeremiah 29:26 speaks of putting someone "in prison and in chains," where the instrument and the chains go together.
2. By extension, the word designates the place where prisoners are confined, the detention house itself. In 2 Chronicles 16:10, Asa has the seer put "in prison": it is the building where he is confined. Similarly, in Jeremiah 20:2, Pasher puts Jeremiah "in the prison that was at the upper gate of Benjamin" — a specific room in the house of the Lord where captives were kept.
H4115.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to overturn," "to turn," "to twist." The starting image is that of something or a body being made to topple, to bend, to twist awkwardly. From there, the name designates the instrument that produces this contortion — the stocks — and then the place where this punishment is applied.
H4115.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, only in the historical and prophetic books (2 Chronicles and Jeremiah). It always designates a place of detention, often associated with physical punishment. In 2 Chronicles 16:10, it is the place where Asa imprisons the seer who rebuked him. In Jeremiah 20:2-3, it is a room in the temple where Pasher confines the prophet Jeremiah after striking him. In Jeremiah 29:26, "prison and chains" are mentioned together, showing that detention is accompanied by physical suffering. The biblical context shows that it is a serious punishment, often inflicted on prophets or political adversaries.
H4115.portee: This prison reminds the reader that the prophets of the Lord often suffered persecution for speaking the truth. Jeremiah, imprisoned and beaten, illustrates the cost of faithful testimony. For the believer, it is a lesson: faithfulness to God can bring suffering and rejection from the world, but God does not abandon him (Jeremiah comes out alive and receives a word from the Lord).

sens: To hurry, to go without delay
To rush, to hasten to accomplish an action
To act with haste or impulsiveness
To express urgency or impatience
H4116A.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is to move or act quickly, without delay. Abraham "quickly goes to his tent" to prepare the meal (Genesis 18:6), and Joshua commands the men to "hurry" across the Jordan (Joshua 4:10): the emphasis is on the acceleration of movement or action.
2. The word also describes the haste of someone who rushes to accomplish something urgently. The woman in Proverbs 7:23 "hurries" to the trap of the seducer, driven by the impulse of the moment. Here, the idea of a rapid momentum, sometimes without reflection, emerges.
3. The word can evoke impulsiveness, even a lack of judgment. Isaiah 5:19 speaks of those who "hasten" the coming of the Almighty, meaning they boldly challenge Him; Proverbs 1:16 reminds us that "the feet of the wicked hurry to evil": haste reflects guilty eagerness.
4. In prayers, the word expresses passionate urgency. The psalmist cries, "hurry to answer me!" (Psalms 69:18), imploring God to intervene without delay in distress, revealing the intensity of need and impatience in waiting.
H4116A.origine: The Hebrew verb מָהַר (mahar) evokes the image of acceleration, of shortening time. It is related to the idea of speed and eagerness. The Hebrew Bible conjugates it in different forms: the Qal (simple form) means "to hurry, to go quickly," the Niphal expresses the idea of being driven by haste, and the Piel reinforces the meaning by marking the urgency or command to act quickly. The word belongs to a family of expressions that all highlight accelerated movement and the absence of delay.
H4116A.emploi: This verb appears 64 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in narratives (Genesis, Samuel, Kings), the Psalms, and the Prophets. It is used for urgent material actions: Abraham prepares the meal "quickly" (Genesis 18:6), Abimelech "hurries" to build a tower (Judges 9:48), or Pharaoh "hurries" to send Israel away (Exodus 12:33). It is also used for attitudes: praying to God with urgency (Psalms 69:18), moving toward sin or rebellion impulsively (Proverbs 1:16). The word translates either a quick and willing obedience or a panicked flight, or an impulsive or guilty urge. In prayers, it asks God to intervene as soon as possible.
H4116A.portee: This word teaches the reader that the speed of action is never neutral: it reveals the intentions of the heart. When one "hurries" to serve (like Abraham), it is a sign of eager generosity; when one "hurries" their steps toward evil, it marks the enslavement to sin. For the believer, learning to hasten their steps toward God and to pray with that same urgency is to recognize that there is no time to lose: life is short, grace is precious, and communion with God does not tolerate delay.

sens: To give money or goods in compensation to obtain something
To pay the bride price for a young girl in marriage
To acquire the right to marry a woman through a required payment
H4117.detail: 1. The word designates the action of paying a sum or giving goods to obtain something in return — it is a purchase or compensation. 2. In a marital context, it is the price that the groom must pay to the family of the young girl to obtain her in marriage: it is the "dowry" or "mohar" (bride price). Exodus 22:16 clearly shows this: the man who seduces an unengaged virgin must "pay her dowry" and marry her — he repairs his wrong by fulfilling this obligation. This system was common in the ancient Near East: the groom would give goods to the family of the young girl, which financed her marriage and protected her economically.
H4117.origine: The Hebrew verb mahár comes from a root meaning "to pay a price" or "to acquire by purchase." The basic image is that of a commercial exchange: giving something of value to receive something else. In biblical culture, this term specialized in the context of marriage to designate the mandatory payment by the groom — an act that legitimized the union and protected the wife.
H4117.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Exodus 22:16. It occurs in the law of forced marriage: if a man seduces a young virgin who is not engaged, he must "pay her dowry" and marry her — this is the repair and regularization of the fault. This context shows that the payment of the dowry was a legal obligation, an act that transformed an illegitimate relationship into a valid marriage and protected the woman by guaranteeing her status as a legitimate wife and the rights that came with it.
H4117.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, marriage is based on concrete material and legal commitments, not just on feeling. The groom assumes an economic responsibility toward his wife: he acknowledges her value and assures her of his commitment. For the modern believer, this underscores that Christian love is also expressed through concrete acts and sacrifices, not just through beautiful words.

sens: That is done quickly, without delay
Haste, speed of execution
Pressing urgency
H4118A.detail: 1. The word describes what happens or is done quickly, without dragging. It is a simple speed: the day of Judgment comes "in all haste," meaning without delay, pressed (Zephaniah 1:14). 2. It is also the eagerness, the haste with which one acts or things occur. One can do something "in haste," quickly done, without taking time. 3. Finally, it is the feeling of urgency, of pressure: when something happens "in haste," it creates tension, one feels that the moment is imminent and inevitable.
H4118A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to hurry" or "to go quickly." It is an adjective or adverb, derived from a form that reinforces the idea of rapid movement. It is found in other words of the same family that all express speed and urgency, the precipitation of the moment.
H4118A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible in this sense, in the book of Zephaniah, where the prophet describes the arrival of the day of Judgment. He characterizes it with certainty and imminence: the day does not delay, it comes without delay, everything converges toward its arrival. This usage places the reader before the urgency of the prophetic threat.
H4118A.portee: The word "haste" reminds us that God's judgment is not a distant and vague event, but something close and pressing. This urgency calls the reader to vigilance and repentance: do not wait, turn to God now. It is a word of awareness in a context of crisis.

sens: Without delay, at a brisk pace
With eagerness, without hesitation
With speed of execution
H4118B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is one of speed: doing something without delay, at a brisk pace. In Exodus 32:8, the people "promptly" turned away from the way by worshiping the golden calf — this happened in just a few days, as Israel was quick to infidelity. Deuteronomy 9:3 also shows this swiftness: the Lord will destroy them "promptly," meaning without dragging his feet.
2. The word also suggests eagerness, the fervor with which one acts. In Joshua 2:5, the men cry, "hurry to pursue them," calling for an immediate and zealous pursuit. It is less about speed than about not hesitating, about getting to work without delay.
3. Finally, it expresses promptness in the execution of a judgment or divine action. Deuteronomy 7:4 speaks of the Lord's "prompt" destruction: it conveys the idea of a decisive and swift action, not of slowness.
H4118B.origine: The Hebrew word מַהֵר (maher) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to hurry, to go quickly." This root expresses the idea of speed and movement without delay. It is linked to the image of someone who does not linger, who quickens their pace. It appears in nominal and verbal forms used throughout the Old Testament to mean "haste" or "precipitation."
H4118B.emploi: This word appears 12 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of the Pentateuch (Exodus, Deuteronomy) and in the historical books (Joshua, Judges). It describes both human action — quickly turning away from the right path (Exodus 32:8, Deuteronomy 9:16) — and divine action — the Lord executing his judgments without delay (Deuteronomy 7:4, 9:3). Sometimes, it introduces a nuance of disrespect or rashness (Israel's hasty infidelity), and sometimes that of effective justice (God's swift punishment). Its use in Judges 2:23 shows the Lord who does not "hasten" to drive out the nations — here the absence of promptness reveals a deliberate patience.
H4118B.portee: This word reminds us that the choices of God, like those of men, can be revealed by their promptness: the speed with which Israel turned away from God shows the fragility of human faith in the face of temptation. Conversely, the promptness of divine judgment affirms that God acts with certainty and without hesitation. This invites the reader to examine their own reactions: are we prompt in obedience as Israel was in disobedience?

sens: Sum of money or gifts paid by the suitor to the father of the young girl to obtain her in marriage
Financial compensation due if the marriage does not take place
Regulated price required in case of seduction
H4119.detail:
1. The dowry (or mohar in Hebrew) is the payment that a man must give to the father of his future wife to obtain her hand in marriage. It is a common practice in ancient Israel, intended to compensate the father for the loss of a daughter and to value the union. Laban thus demands a "large dowry" and many gifts from Shechem who wants to marry his daughter (Genesis 34:12).
2. This dowry also represents a legal protection for the young girl: if a man seduces her without the intention of marrying her, he must pay the parents a dowry equivalent to that of a virgin, even if he does not marry her (Exodus 22:17).
3. King Saul turns it into a political challenge: instead of a dowry in money or goods, he asks David for a hundred Philistine foreskins, hoping indirectly to have him perish in battle (1 Samuel 18:25).
H4119.origine: The word mohar comes from a root meaning "to pay" or "to reimburse." It literally designates the "price of acquisition" that establishes the husband's right over his wife. It is a typical institution of marriage in the ancient Near East, analogous to the "bride-price" of neighboring cultures, distinct from the modern dowry that goes from the father to the bride.
H4119.emploi: The word mohar appears three times in the Segond in matrimonial contexts. In Genesis 34:12, it is a voluntary payment offered by Shechem, who is enamored with Dina. In Exodus 22:17, it is a legal obligation imposed on the seducer. In 1 Samuel 18:25, Saul diverts its use for hostile purposes, substituting a military act for a payment. The word reinforces the idea that marriage in ancient Israel is an economic contract engaging the husband's responsibility toward the woman's family.
H4119.portee: The concept of dowry helps us understand how the Bible views marriage: not as a private sentiment, but as a public and contractual act that binds two families. It also shows that women, although married, remained protected by a recognized economic value, which limited the husband's arbitrariness. For the modern believer, this reminds us that marriage is a serious and costly covenant, not a mere fleeting affection.

sens: Action of hurrying, doing something without delay
Speed, quickness of execution
Character of what happens or is done without delay
Urgency that drives to act
H4120.detail:
1. Promptness primarily means to act quickly, without delay: it is the act of hurrying, moving without waiting. In Numbers 16:46, Moses orders Aaron to go "promptly" to the assembly with the incense to stop the plague; it is about not losing a moment in the face of urgency.
2. The word also expresses the speed with which an action is accomplished or realized. The psalmists speak of the swiftness with which the wicked wither: "they are cut down as quickly as the grass" (Psalms 37:2).
3. Promptness can denote the absence of delay in executing a sentence or consequence. In Ecclesiastes 8:11, the preacher observes that due to the lack of swift punishment of the wicked, the hearts of men are filled with the desire to do evil.
4. The word finally emphasizes the urgency that drives to act immediately. In Joshua 10:6, the Gibeonites plead with Joshua to come "quickly" to rescue them: the enemy is there, danger presses.
H4120.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to hurry" or "to go quickly." It is related to the idea of rapid and spontaneous movement. It is a feminine noun that captures the state of urgency or the quality of speed: not just going fast once, but having this quality of promptness. The word appears in various biblical contexts where time matters: danger, God's anger, an opportunity that slips away.
H4120.emploi: This word appears about 20 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in action narratives (Samuel, Joshua), but also in wisdom poetry (Psalms, Ecclesiastes) and the prophets. In military or crisis contexts, it expresses urgency: Moses and Aaron must act quickly to stop the judgment, Joshua must hasten to rescue. In the Psalms, it describes the rapidity of natural or divine phenomena: the destruction of the wicked, the swiftness of God's word. In Ecclesiastes, it serves to show that the absence of promptness in punishment encourages evil. The word can be used as an adverb ("promptly," "quickly") or with a preposition ("in haste"), always to mark urgency or the absence of delay.
H4120.portee: For the believer, the word promptness reminds us that certain moments require immediate action without hesitation: responding to God's call, fleeing sin, helping those in need. It also emphasizes that God himself acts with speed and justice, and that the absence of swift consequences does not mean the absence of judgment. It is an exhortation to vigilance and obedience without delay.

sens: Warrior of David, from Nethopha
H4121.detail: Maharaï is a man who lived during the united monarchy of Israel. He is first mentioned in 2 Samuel 23:28 as one of David's mighty warriors, originating from the city of Nethopha in Judah. He also appears in 1 Chronicles 11:30 in a similar list of these strong men of the king. Finally, in 1 Chronicles 27:13, we learn that he commanded the military division of the tenth month and belonged to the family of the Zerahites, with twenty-four thousand men under his command.
H4121.origine: The name Maharaï means "impetuous" in Hebrew, suggesting a man of action and vigor. It reflects the character of this warrior established in Nethopha, a locality in the territory of Judah.
H4121.emploi: Maharaï is mentioned three times in the Bible, always in relation to David and the organization of his army. In 2 Samuel 23:28, he is listed among the thirty most valiant warriors of King David. In 1 Chronicles 11:30, he is found in a parallel enumeration of these same strong men. In 1 Chronicles 27:13, the context changes: we see Maharaï in an administrative and military role, commanding a division of twenty-four thousand men for the tenth month of the royal calendar, which shows that he grew in responsibility in service to the king.

sens: Son of the prophet Isaiah
Child bearing a symbolic prophetic name
Living sign of God's promise regarding the destruction of enemy kingdoms
H4122.detail:
1. Maher-Schalal-Chasch-Baz is the son of the prophet Isaiah, first mentioned in Isaiah 8:1. He has an older brother, Shear-Jashub, another son of the prophet.

2. His name is not a simple appellation: it is a prophetic name given by the command of the Lord Himself. In Isaiah 8:3, the Lord commands the prophet to give his son this particular name: "Call his name Maher-Schalal-Chasch-Baz."

3. The name means "the spoil hastens, the prey speeds" (or "the spoil is swift, the prey rushes"). It is a prophetic announcement: before the child is old enough to speak, the kingdoms of Damascus and Samaria will be plundered and carried away by the king of Assyria. The child himself, through his existence and name, becomes a living sign of the fulfillment of God's promise.
H4122.origine: The Hebrew name "Maher-Shalal-Chash-Baz" is composed of four words: "maher" (swift, prompt), "shalal" (spoil, plunder), "chash" (to hasten, press), and "baz" (spoil, prey). It is a very poetic and symbolic construction, typical of how Isaiah designates his children as signs from God. The prophet had already given his first son the name Shear-Jashub ("a remnant will return"), and he will later give this third son a name composed of four terms that together proclaim the imminence of divine destruction.
H4122.emploi: Maher-Schalal-Chasch-Baz is named only twice in the Bible, both in Isaiah 8. He first appears in Isaiah 8:1, where the Lord commands Isaiah to write the name on a tablet as a public and clear testimony. Then, in Isaiah 8:3, it is the prophetess (Isaiah's wife) who conceives and bears this son, and the Lord prescribes to the prophet to give him this prophetic name. This rarity of mentions underscores the highly symbolic and prophetic nature of this child: he is reported in Scripture only as a bearer of a sign from God for his time.
H4122.portee: Maher-Schalal-Chasch-Baz teaches the believer that God does not merely speak: He acts and makes His promises visible, even through the most ordinary human lives. A child becomes, through his name given by God, a living and irrefutable sign of what God will do. For the contemporary reader of Isaiah, every time this child was called by his name, the promise of the fall of Damascus and Samaria was recalled. It is an invitation to recognize that God governs history and keeps His promises, even when they seem distant.

sens: Deceptive vision or unfounded illusion
Pleasant but false lie
Flattering word intended to deceive
H4123.detail:
1. The word refers to a vision or word that has no reality, an illusion created to seduce the mind. It is something that seems beautiful or true at first glance, but does not correspond to any deep truth. In Isaiah 30:10, people ask the prophets to prophesy "chimères" instead of truths: they want to be deceived rather than hear reality.
2. The word emphasizes the pleasant lie, one that flatters the listener to please them. It is a false word intentionally spoken to satisfy the listener's desire for illusion — like those who prefer a sweet vision to hard truth.
H4123.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "slipping" or "deviating," making it a natural image for deception: a discourse that leads you away from the path of truth. It is related to other Hebrew words denoting seduction or error. This family of words underscores how lies divert the mind from reality.
H4123.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 30:10. The prophet Isaiah denounces the Israelites who refuse the true oracles of God and ask the seers and prophets to tell them "chimères" — sweet and flattering words instead of the harsh truths they need to hear. It is a word of denunciation: the prophet highlights how one prefers to deceive oneself rather than confront the facts.
H4123.portee: This word warns against our natural tendency to prefer comforting lies over uncomfortable truths. It reminds us that rejecting God's word for pleasant "chimères" is a form of rebellion. It is an invitation to seek the truth, even when it disturbs us.

sens: Region and people located east of the Jordan, descendants of Lot
Monarchical state and political power rivaling Israel
Idolatrous people worshiping Chemosh as their national god
H4124G.detail:
1. Moab is primarily the name of the territory occupied by the descendants of Lot's son (see Genesis 36:35 and Deuteronomy 2:8). It is a mountainous region east of the Jordan, between the Jordan and the Arabian desert, bordering Israel.

2. Moab later becomes a kingdom with its own king and fortified cities. During the time of the judges and the monarchy, Moab is a powerful neighbor: sometimes a vassal (2 Samuel 8:2), sometimes in revolt, it engages in battles against Israel (2 Kings 3:4-5, Judges 3:12-14) and can even temporarily oppress Israel.

3. Moab is an idolatrous people whose main deity is Chemosh (2 Kings 23:13: "Chemosh, the abomination of Moab"). This religious trait also appears in the story of Ruth, a converted Moabite (Ruth 2:6), which shows that Scripture does not reject the Moabite people themselves but their idolatry.
H4124G.origine: The name Moab literally means "from his father" in Hebrew. According to Genesis 19:37, Moab is the son that Lot had through incest with his eldest daughter. Although Moab comes from a reprehensible union, his name preserves this genealogy: it designates the entire people descended from him. The link with Lot, the father of Israel through Abraham according to biblical genealogies, establishes a distant kinship between the two peoples.
H4124G.emploi: Moab appears 145 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in Exodus, Numbers, the historical books (Judges, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), and the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah). During the Exodus, Moab fears Israel as they cross the desert (Numbers 22:3-4, Exodus 15:15); Balaam is hired to curse Israel from Moab (Numbers 22-24). In the time of the judges, Eglon of Moab oppresses Israel (Judges 3:12-30). Under the monarchy, Moab is alternately subdued (2 Samuel 8:2) or revolted (2 Kings 3:4-5), leading to military campaigns. The prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah pronounce oracles against Moab, threatening the people for their pride (Isaiah 16:6) and their lack of repentance (Jeremiah 48:28). The last king, Moses, dies in view of the land of Moab (Deuteronomy 34:5-6).
H4124G.portee: Moab reminds the reader that God governs distant nations and makes Israel's enemies bow before Him. Furthermore, the very existence of Moab, an idolatrous people located at the border of God's people, illustrates the contrast between those who worship the true God and those who turn to false gods. The story of Ruth, a Moabite who abandons the gods of her people to turn to the God of Israel, shows that even distant nations can embrace faith in God and find a place in His story of salvation.

sens: son of Lot and his eldest daughter
nation descended from Moab
territory inhabited by the Moabites
H4124H.detail:
1. Moab is the son that Lot's eldest daughter bore after the destruction of Sodom (Genesis 19:37). His name means "from his father" in Hebrew, as he was born from a union between Lot and his own daughter. This character marks the beginning of the genealogy of the Moabites.
2. By extension, Moab designates the entire people descended from this first Moab, the Moabites. This people occupies an important place in biblical history as a neighbor and sometimes adversary of Israel.
3. Moab also refers to the territory inhabited by this people, east of the Jordan, a fertile region well-defined in the geography of ancient Levant.
H4124H.origine: The name Moab literally means "from his father" in Hebrew (mô = "from" and av = "father"). This etymology reflects the circumstances of his birth: he is the result of an incestuous relationship between Lot and his eldest daughter, preserved in Genesis 19 as an origin narrative attesting to the distant kinship between Israel and the Moabite people.
H4124H.emploi: Moab first appears as the eponymous ancestor of the Moabite people at his birth in Genesis 19:37. Subsequently, the name Moab is used to designate the people of the Moabites, who form with Israel a group of peoples related through Lot (uncle of Judah and Israel). The kingdom of Moab becomes an important state in ancient Levant, mentioned in contexts of wars, alliances, and conflicts with Israel in the books of Judges, Samuel, and Kings. Its inhabitants and territory play a recurring role in the political and religious life of Israel.
H4124H.portee: The account of Moab's origins, marked by incest, reveals how the biblical author assumes a candid view of the genealogies of neighboring peoples, including dishonorable origins. This underscores that genealogical proximity to Israel does not imply moral affinity or lasting alliance: Moab will alternately be a rival, ally, or adversary depending on historical circumstances. For the reader, this teaches that God's choice of Israel does not rest on blood or carnal kinship.

sens: Fertile region east of the Jordan, southeast of the Dead Sea
People descended from Moab, son of Lot
Kingdom established in this region
H4124I.detail:
1. Moab refers to a fertile and flat region of Transjordan, east of the Jordan, known for its "plains" (the Hebrew term literally means "plains of Moab"). It is here that the children of Israel camped during their last stop before entering the Promised Land, as shown in Numbers 33:48: "They departed from the mountains of Abarim and camped in the plains of Moab, near the Jordan, opposite Jericho."
2. The term also designates the Moabite people, descendants of Moab, son of Lot (according to Genesis). This people occupied this region and formed a distinct nation from Israel.
3. By extension, Moab can refer to the Moabite kingdom or state itself, with its own political and religious structures, distinct from other kingdoms in the region.
H4124I.origine: The Hebrew name Moab means "from his father" or "from my father." According to Genesis, Moab was the eldest son of Lot, who was himself the nephew of Abraham. The region bears the name of this eponymous ancestor. The term "plains of Moab" (Araboth Moab) combines the word for "plains" and the name of the region, specifically designating the flat and fertile territory that the Moabite people occupied east of the Jordan.
H4124I.emploi: Moab appears about 12 times in the provided usages, exclusively in the Pentateuch and early in the book of Joshua. The Bible consistently locates the plains of Moab "near the Jordan, opposite Jericho" (Numbers 22:1, 26:63, 33:48, 33:50; Deuteronomy 34:8). It is in this region that Moses gives the last laws to the Israelites (Deuteronomy 34:1) and where he dies (Deuteronomy 34:8). The text also evokes the sad events that took place there, notably Israel's apostasy with the daughters of Moab (Numbers 25, implicitly mentioned by the context of these encampments). Moab thus remains the transitional place between wandering in the desert and entering the Promised Land.
H4124I.portee: The stay in the plains of Moab carries significant theological importance: it is the threshold of the fulfillment of the promises made to the patriarchs. This region embodies both the imminence of deliverance and the ultimate test of faith — Israel coexists with an idolatrous people and must resist religious seduction (the worship of Baal-Peor) before finally crossing the Jordan. For the Christian reader, Moab serves as a reminder that the fulfillment of God's promises requires perseverance and sanctification until the end.

sens: Inhabitant or inhabitant of the land of Moab
Person from Moab, descendant of the Moabites
H4125.detail: A Moabite is a person from the kingdom of Moab, located east of the Jordan River, in present-day Jordan. Ruth is referred to as "the Moabite" (Ruth 1:22; Ruth 4:5) to highlight her foreign origins, although she becomes the wife of Boaz and the ancestor of King David. The term refers to both the inhabitants of the land and those who descend from them, even if they live elsewhere.
H4125.origine: The Hebrew word "Moabite" (moabi) comes from Moab, the name of the land and its eponymous ancestor. According to Genesis, Moab was the son of Lot and his eldest daughter. The name "Moab" likely means "from the father" or "who comes from the father," recalling the shameful origin of the people according to the biblical account. The Moabites are one of Israel's brother nations through the line of Lot, Abraham's cousin.
H4125.emploi: The word "Moabite" appears about 16 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Law (Deuteronomy), in the book of Ruth, and in historical accounts. In Deuteronomy 23:3, it is stated that a Moabite cannot enter the assembly of the Lord. However, Ruth the Moabite becomes a remarkable exception: she marries Boaz and enters into the inheritance of Israel, showing that faith can transcend ethnic and religious barriers. King Solomon will marry Moabite women among other nations (1 Kings 11:1).
H4125.portee: The story of Ruth the Moabite teaches that God welcomes those who turn to Him in faith, regardless of their origin or religious past. Although the Law prohibited Moabites from entering the assembly, Ruth finds grace through her faithfulness to God and Naomi. She thus becomes a powerful symbol of redemption by grace and the inclusion of the foreigner in God's salvific plan.

sens: Opening or passage through which one enters a place
Action of entering, movement of entry
Way of presenting oneself, demeanor, behavior
H4126.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the physical opening, passage, or access point in a building or enclosed space. In Ezekiel 43:11, it refers to the entrances of the temple, the doors and accesses through which one enters the holy house.
2. It also signifies the concrete action of entering somewhere, the act of crossing a threshold or space. It is the movement itself, the arrival of someone in a place.
3. By extension, the word can refer to the manner in which someone conducts themselves, their demeanor, their public behavior. In 2 Samuel 3:25, Joab speaks of Abner's "ways," meaning his way of acting and presenting himself, suggesting that Abner is coming to spy on him.
H4126.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root בוא (bo'a), which means "to enter, to come." The prefix מ (m), transformed into מו (mo) before a vowel, indicates the place or action, hence literally "the act of entering" or "the place of entry." This root is very common in the Bible and appears in related forms denoting arrival or access.
H4126.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible. In 2 Samuel 3:25, it describes the comings and goings, the demeanor of Abner, his behavior and movements—the idea being that someone observes how he acts. In Ezekiel 43:11, it concretely refers to the entrances of the temple, the passages and doors through which one enters. The meaning thus varies between the action or manner of entering (behavior) and the physical place of entry (architectural opening).
H4126.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that our entries and exits, our manner of presenting and acting, are observed and matter before God. It also emphasizes the importance of access to God's dwelling: the temple has its specific entrances, just as the Church today has its conditions of access in Christ. It is an invitation to be vigilant about our spiritual walk.

sens: Liquefy something solid by heat or the action of time
Tremble, lose firmness or assurance
Faint, collapse from fear or emotion
Be annihilated, dispersed, reduced to nothing
H4127.detail:
1. To melt: the literal meaning of the word, transforming solid matter into liquid, like wax or snow in the sun (Psalms 65:11 speaks of "mountains covered with wheat that wave"... no, let's start over). The word evokes the idea of dissolution, of loss of consistency. Although this concrete meaning is rare in the provided texts, it illuminates all the others.

2. To tremble: this is the most frequent usage. A city or land "trembles" when it loses its stability in the face of threat, like Damascus which "trembles" upon hearing bad news (Jeremiah 49:23), or the whole earth which "trembles" when the Lord touches it (Amos 9:5). This is not a violent shaking, but a loss of solidity, as if the foundations were giving way.

3. To be seized with fear, to be paralyzed: when the inhabitants of the land "are seized" by terror in front of the Israelites (Joshua 2:9), the verb describes the horror that freezes the heart and removes all capacity for reaction. It is a fear that liquefies the will.

4. To be annihilated, dissipated: Job cries that God "annihilates" him at the sound of the storm (Job 30:22), deploying the image of one who is melted, dispersed, reduced to nothing by divine force. It is complete dissolution, physical or moral.
H4127.origine: The Hebrew root מוּג describes the action of losing shape, rigidity, solidity—the opposite movement of consolidation. It likely has as its first image the melting of a malleable substance. The word belongs to a family of Hebrew verbs that express movements of dissolution or failure: the idea of "to collapse" or "to fall apart" is found. In biblical Hebrew, this verb is mostly used with God as the subject (He who melts) or the earth, cities, peoples as the subject (they who tremble).
H4127.emploi: The verb מוּג appears 17 times in the provided Old Testament, mainly in the poetic and prophetic books (Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah) and in accounts of divine intervention (Joshua, Amos). It is almost always used in the sense of "to tremble" or "to be seized with fear": peoples tremble before God or before an enemy threat, the earth trembles at the voice of the Lord. Sometimes it takes on a shade of "annihilation" (Job 30:22), showing that trembling leads to destruction. The subject can be concrete (the earth, a door, the inhabitants) or abstract (the confidence of enemies). The underlying idea is always one of loss of solidity, of internal or external collapse.
H4127.portee: This word reveals how the Bible conceives of fear and weakness: not as fleeting feelings, but as a dissolution of self, a liquefaction of the ability to stand firm. For a believer, seeing the earth "melt" before the Lord (Amos 9:5) reminds us that only God is stable and unshakeable; everything else—our fears, our enemies, even creation—can be reduced to nothing by His presence. It is an invitation not to tremble before what passes, but to ground our assurance in the One who alone remains.

sens: Examine or evaluate by sight
Shake or make tremble
H4128.detail:
1. To measure means to carefully examine something in order to evaluate it. Here, it is the eye that measures: in Habakkuk 3:6, the prophet sees God who with His eye "measures" the earth — He observes, contemplates, and evaluates it with a gaze that weighs and scrutinizes, before making the nations tremble.
2. At its root, the word also evokes the idea of shaking or making tremble: it is an image of movement and power. The same verb can describe the action of shaking, agitating, or vibrating; it is through this power that one "measures" creation, subjecting it to His inspection.
H4128.origine: The Hebrew word mud comes from a root that carries the idea of shaking, agitating, or oscillating. The form used here (Polel) is an intensive or repeated form of the verb, reinforcing the idea of action. In biblical Hebrew, the same root appears in words evoking movement and instability. It is an image of the divine power that stirs and evaluates all that it looks upon.
H4128.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Habakkuk 3:6. In this context of theophany — the powerful manifestation of God — the verb describes the sovereign gaze of the Lord upon creation. It is a gaze that is not passive: it measures, weighs, judges, and His mere presence makes the mountains tremble and the hills bow down. The unique usage underscores the exceptional nature of this moment when God contemplates His work to evaluate and transform it.
H4128.portee: This word invites the believer to meditate on the gaze of God: it is not an indifferent gaze, but one that scrutinizes, measures, and evaluates everything with justice. It reminds us that nothing escapes divine vigilance and that the power of this gaze is sufficient to transform the order of the world. For the reader, it is an assurance that God fully masters His creation.

sens: person linked by blood or family
close friend, like a family member
H4129.detail:
1. The word designates a person who belongs to the same family, either by blood or by marriage. In Ruth 2:1, Boaz is a "relative" of Elimelech, meaning a close relative of the family, a man from the family circle to whom one can entrust their affairs.
2. The word also extends to someone treated with the familiarity and tenderness of a family member. In Proverbs 7:4, wisdom is called a "friend," as one would for a beloved sister, to show total intimacy and trust.
H4129.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to know." A relative or friend is someone you know well, whom you have been close to for a long time, and who is familiar to you. This image of familiarity and knowledge is at the heart of the word: it is someone with whom you have a true established relationship.
H4129.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Ruth 2:1, it refers to a relative in the strict sense, a family member with whom one shares blood or marriage ties, and from whom one can expect help and support according to family solidarity customs. In Proverbs 7:4, the wise man uses it figuratively to express a personal relationship of intimacy with wisdom and understanding: they are treated as close ones, as constant companions to whom one confides.
H4129.portee: This word reminds us that true human relationships, whether familial or friendly, rest on mutual knowledge and deep familiarity. For the believer, it invites cultivating this intimacy with God's wisdom, treating it as one would treat a sister, making it a living presence in daily life.

sens: One who is related to someone by blood or family
Kinship, family bond
The entire group of close relatives of a family
H4130.detail:
1. This word designates one who belongs to the same family, a relative in a broad sense — uncle, cousin, nephew, or close relative. In Ruth 3:2, Naomi refers to Boaz as a "relative," meaning someone from the clan or kin of her husband, someone from the same family household who can help her according to Israelite law.
2. The word evokes kinship and the sense of bond that unites members of the same family. This includes the moral and legal obligation to help each other, to be responsible for one another — a solidarity of blood and household.
3. In the Israelite context, it refers to the entire group of close ones forming the clan or extended family, a group to which one belongs by birth and which has rights and duties among its members.
H4130.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to know" or "to recognize" — the underlying idea is that a relative is someone you "know" because they belong to the family, someone you recognize as your own. This is why the word designates the kinship bond as a recognized and established fact among the members of a household.
H4130.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the book of Ruth. It is used to describe Boaz from Naomi's perspective: he is a relative capable of playing the role of "redeemer," meaning someone who has the right and duty, according to Israelite custom, to help a widow and a child of his family. The context shows that kinship involved specific legal obligations.
H4130.portee: This word reminds us that in biblical thought, family is not just affection, but responsibility. To be a relative is to be bound by the obligation to help one's own. For the reader, this sheds light on how God envisioned social order: through the care that close ones must have for one another, not through abandonment.

sens: Lose balance, topple, collapse
Be shaken, stirred, agitated
Be morally destabilized, doubt, weaken
Fall, crumble, disappear
(Causative) Make fall, dislodge, overturn
H4131.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of a person or thing losing footing: their legs give way, they wobble on their foundations. In Leviticus 25:35, "his hand falters" evokes someone who is weakening, whose strength is failing.
2. Shaken describes the state of something that is shaken by an external force — a mountain trembling, the earth agitated by an earthquake. In Psalms 46:3, the mountains "stagger at the heart of the seas" under the effect of a power that shakes them.
3. In a moral and spiritual sense, to stagger means to doubt, to weaken in one's trust or faith: not to remain unshaken in the face of trials. In Psalms 15:5 and 62:3, the one who never staggers is presented as stable, unshaken, firmly established.
4. To fall or crumble is the culmination of staggering: what cannot be shaken will never fall. In Psalms 104:5, the earth "will never be shaken" because God has established it on solid foundations.
5. When the verb is used causatively, it means to actively make something fall, to dislodge something from its stable place — an action of force that overturns what was established.
H4131.origine: The root מוט (mot) evokes the fundamental idea of unstable movement, of toppling: something that is not fixed, that moves when one expects it to remain still. This verb belongs to a lexical field of instability and trembling. In the Old Testament, it regularly contrasts with the solidity of what is "established" or "firmed" by God — a theological motif: only what God founds cannot stagger.
H4131.emploi: The verb mot appears 36 times in the Old Testament, very frequently in the Psalms (27 times), where it denotes either the physical shaking of creation (earth, mountains) or the spiritual stability of the righteous in the face of trials. It is also found in Proverbs (image of the solidity of the path of the righteous), in Isaiah (future destruction of creation), and in only one verse of the Torah (Leviticus 25:35, regarding impoverishment). The word carries a nuance of threatening instability everywhere and contrasts with the unwavering trust in God: the one who does not stagger is the one who relies on the Lord as on an unshakable rock.
H4131.portee: This verb teaches the reader that stability — in faith, morality, life — does not come from us, but from our attachment to God who never moves. Every time the Bible says "you will not stagger," it affirms that the one who truly trusts in God remains standing despite the tremors of the world. It is a promise for the believer's heart: when everything shakes around him, he can remain unshaken.

sens: Bar or pole used to carry or transport something
Piece of wood that connects draft animals and to which the yoke is attached
Trembling, swaying, instability
State of subjugation or servitude
H4132.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a wooden bar, a pole placed on the shoulders to carry a burden for two: it is a stretcher. In Numbers 13:23, the spies bring back a branch of grapes "by means of a pole" — they carry it together by suspending it on this bar between their shoulders. In Numbers 4:10-12, the stretcher is used to transport the utensils of the sanctuary, wrapped and protected: it is heavy material that cannot be held in hand.
2. The word also refers to the yoke itself, this piece of wood carried by a draft animal (ox, donkey) that connects it to a companion or a vehicle. Nahum 1:13 promises to break the yoke of oppression: "I will break its yoke off you."
3. Figuratively, "to stagger" evokes instability: in Psalms 66:9 and 121:3, the foot that "stumbles" is a foot that sways, lacking firmness. It is the opposite image of stability and trust.
4. In a spiritual sense, the yoke symbolizes servitude, domination, the weight of external oppression. Breaking the yoke means tearing someone away from servitude.
H4132.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a primitive root suggesting movement, swaying. The basic image is that of swaying, trembling — like a bar that oscillates or a yoke that weighs on the neck. From this arise the two families of meaning: the concrete (the bar carried, the animal yoke) and the abstract (what sways, what weighs, what oppresses). Hebrew retains this dual meaning in a single word, like many biblical terms that blend physical imagery with its moral echo.
H4132.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible. First in Numbers 4:10 and 4:12, where it refers to the stretcher used for the ritual transport of the objects of the sanctuary — this is its most concrete sense. In Numbers 13:23, it is the pole between the shoulders of the two spies. Then, in the Psalms, it takes on the color of swaying: Psalms 66:9 and 121:3 use the verb "to stumble" to say that God prevents our foot from slipping or sliding. Finally, Nahum 1:13 uses it in the spiritual sense of the oppressive yoke: it is the burden of servitude that God promises to remove from His people. The word thus glides from material transport to physical stability, then to moral subjugation.
H4132.portee: This word teaches us that God knows the weight of our burdens — both material loads and the invisible yoke of servitude. It also reminds us that our foot will not slip if we lean on Him: it is a promise of moral and spiritual stability amid trials. Finally, it announces that God can break any yoke — there is a possible freedom, a deliverance that only God can give.

sens: Piece of wood that connects two draft animals or rests on the neck of a beast to pull a load
Bar or beam serving as support or attachment point
Oppression, servitude, enslavement
H4133.detail:
1. The yoke is primarily a concrete object: the piece of wood placed on the shoulders or neck of draft animals to harness them together or to make them pull a weight. In 1 Chronicles 15:15, the yoke refers to the wooden bars that allowed the Levites to carry the ark of God on their shoulders.
2. By extension, the word applies to any rigid bar used for support or maintenance: a beam, a crosspiece of framework or equipment.
3. In a figurative sense, very common in the prophets, the yoke becomes the image of oppression and servitude. When the Lord says in Leviticus 26:13 that He has "broken the bonds of your yoke," He means that He has freed Israel from slavery in Egypt. Isaiah 58:6 and 58:9 use this symbol to speak of breaking the chains of injustice and the weight of oppression that the powerful impose on the weak.
H4133.origine: The Hebrew word motah comes from a root that evokes the idea of a bar or beam. It is a concrete term, drawn from the rural and agricultural life of Israel, where yokes were everyday tools.
