The great bronze sea, like all the utensils of the temple, reflected the majesty and holiness of God. This invites us to consider how we honor God in the care we take in our acts of worship.

sens: that which has been poured and solidified in metal to form a unique piece
conduit or pipe through which a liquid or light flows
H4166.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the metal object obtained by casting in a mold: the oxen of the bronze reservoir in the temple, in 2 Chronicles 4:3, are not added afterward; they are "cast" with the basin itself, poured in one piece. It is a very prestigious technique of bronze working.
2. By extension, it also designates a conduit or pipe: the seven "pipes" of the golden lampstand in Zechariah 4:2 are the tubes through which the oil flows to the lamps. The word retains the idea of an elongated and hollow shape, shaped in one go.
H4166.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to melt, to pour." It evokes the action of the caster who pours molten metal into a mold to create a lasting shape. All biblical usages concern objects of the tabernacle or the temple, where the quality of metallurgical work was crucial.
H4166.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 2 Chronicles 4:3, it describes the oxen of the great bronze basin, cast in one piece with the reservoir. In Zechariah 4:2, it designates the conduits of the sacred lampstand. Both contexts concern temple worship and highlight the technical and aesthetic perfection of sacred objects.
H4166.portee: This word reminds us that God cares about the beauty and solidity of things dedicated to Him. The details of worship are never negligible: the refined metallurgical work of the temple reflects the majesty of the One who is worshiped there. For us, this invites us to serve God with excellence and order in all that we do.

sens: To openly ridicule someone in words
To deride with contempt and malice
To criticize someone in a hurtful and haughty manner
H4167.detail:
1. To mock means to make fun of someone out loud, in words, ridiculing them in front of others. It is more than a joke: it is an intentionally hurtful and contemptuous mockery.
2. The word evokes the image of someone speaking maliciously to humiliate and offend. In Psalm 73:8, the wicked "mock": they make fun, speak with contempt, showing their arrogance through haughty speech.
3. To mock also means to criticize someone cruelly and insultingly, publicly belittling them through words to assert one's own superiority.
H4167.origine: The Hebrew root מוּק expresses the idea of speaking with disdain and malice. It belongs to the group of verbs that describe the manner of speaking—not what is said, but how it is said: with mockery, arrogance, and intent to harm. The Hiphil (form used here) reinforces this idea of deliberate and manifest action.
H4167.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 73:8. It describes the behavior of the wicked who prosper despite their wickedness: they mock, they speak with contempt of others, they utter haughty threats. It is a characteristic trait of their proud attitude towards the weak and the righteous whom they seek to oppress.
H4167.portee: This word reminds us that mockery and disdain are forms of spiritual violence. Seeing how the Bible describes the mockery of the wicked helps us recognize this malice within ourselves and resist it, seeking instead kindness and respect towards others, even those we disapprove of.

sens: burning wood, glowing coal
blazing hearth or fire
consuming suffering
devastating divine judgment
H4168.detail:
1. An ember is primarily a piece of wood that is burning or has just burned, still glowing: in Psalm 102:4, the psalmist compares his bones to embers, an image of the pain that burns within him.
2. The word can also refer to a blazing hearth, a bonfire: it conveys the idea of fire that devours and consumes everything in its path.
3. Figuratively, the ember represents inner suffering that gnaws away: the psalmist sees his days vanish into smoke while his bones burn like embers.
4. The ember becomes the image of divine judgment, the devastating punishment: in Isaiah 33:14, the wicked tremble asking who can survive before the eternal flames of God's judgment.
H4168.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes what burns, what is aflame. It belongs to the family of words that denote fire, combustion, and intense heat. The image of the ember—this red coal that persists after the flames have gone out—evokes both destruction and the persistence of fire.
H4168.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalm 102:4, in a personal lament, the ember symbolizes the physical and moral suffering of the afflicted psalmist. In Isaiah 33:14, in a judgment oracle, it designates the terrible flames of God's punishment awaiting the wicked. In both contexts, the ember is never neutral: it is always an image of destruction, consumption, of what ravages.
H4168.portee: This word reminds us that suffering, in the Bible, is often perceived as a fire that burns from within: it is not merely a passing pain, but something that consumes. It also invites us to take seriously the biblical warning about divine judgment: the eternal flames are not an empty threat, but the expression of God's fearsome character in the face of evil.

sens: The upper part of the altar where the fire burns
The domestic hearth, the place of fire that warms and prepares food
H4169.detail:
1. In the context of worship, the hearth is the high surface of the altar where the burnt offering rests overnight. It is there that the fire continues to burn, consuming the offering. In Leviticus 6:2, the hearth of the altar is the burning heart of the sacrifice, kept ablaze from evening to morning to fulfill the offering rite to God.
2. The word also evokes the domestic hearth, the place of fire where food is prepared and cooked, where the family gathers. The image of the constantly burning fire connects temple worship with daily life: both are places where fire transforms and purifies.
H4169.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to light" or "to burn." It is related to words for "fire" and "combustion." The hearth carries the idea of living and continuous warmth, the fire that is maintained so that it never goes out.
H4169.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 6:2, where it specifically designates the surface of the bronze altar. In this passage, the instruction emphasizes that the burnt offering must remain on the hearth all night, the fire never to be extinguished. This underscores the importance of uninterrupted daily worship, where each day begins with the morning offering.
H4169.portee: This word reminds us that worship is not an isolated moment, but a flame that burns continuously. For today's believer, the hearth of the altar symbolizes a constant consecration, a devotion that is never extinguished. It is the biblical image of a heart that continues to seek God, day after day.

sens: Net or hidden device to capture a beast or a person
Hidden danger that threatens to seize us
Words or behavior that lead us to evil
Spiritual trap: being drawn away from God by idols or evil
H4170.detail:
1. In its primary sense, a trap is a physical device — net, snare, bait — set to catch an animal or an enemy without them seeing it coming. The Bible mentions these real traps: a hunter or warrior sets them along the way (Amos 3:5: "Does a bird fall into a trap on the ground when there is no bait?").
2. The trap becomes an image of the invisible danger that threatens us. When Moses warns the people of Israel, he cautions them that the inhabitants of the land will be for you "a net and a trap" (Joshua 23:13), a constant threat from which one can hardly escape.
3. Our own words or foolish actions can be a trap for our soul: "The mouth of the fool brings ruin upon himself, and his lips are a snare for his soul" (Proverbs 18:7). This means that we bring misfortune upon ourselves through our folly.
4. On a spiritual level, the trap refers to anything that distances us from God: foreign idols (Psalms 106:36: "They worshiped their idols, which became a snare to them"), bad company (Proverbs 22:25: "Do not associate with a man given to anger"), or the fear of man rather than trust in God (Proverbs 29:25: "The fear of man lays a snare").
H4170.origine: The Hebrew word *moqesh* comes from a root meaning "to capture" or "to catch." It is related to other words in the same family that all evoke the idea of seizing or holding. The word paints the concrete image of the hunter's trap — something hidden, secret, that one does not see coming and that immobilizes you. This is why the Bible also uses it for spiritual and moral traps: the danger hides its game, one does not see it until one is caught.
H4170.emploi: The word appears 27 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and Proverbs. The Psalms use it to describe the persecutions against the righteous: malicious men set traps for David and the faithful (Psalms 64:6, 141:9). Proverbs uses it to show how wisdom preserves us from the trap while folly rushes us into it: bad company, the fool, the fear of man, imprudence in oaths — all of these set traps (Proverbs 12:13, 18:7, 29:25). Moses warns Israel that the idolatrous peoples will be a trap for him if he imitates them (Exodus 23:33, Deuteronomy 7:16, Joshua 23:13). The context varies: sometimes it is an external danger (enemies), sometimes it is an internal danger (our own words, our choices).
H4170.portee: This word teaches the believer to remain vigilant and clear-sighted: evil does not always present itself head-on; it hides. The Bible teaches us to recognize spiritual traps — the seductions of the world, bad company, fear — so that we do not fall into them. But it also reminds us that wisdom, the fear of the Lord, and trust in God are our protection. Finally, this word warns us against our own words and actions: we are often the first architects of our own misfortune.

sens: Substitute one thing for another, exchange
Transform, alter the state or nature of something
Abandon or renounce a commitment, a promise made
Transform, change state (for a thing)
H4171.detail:
1. **Substituting one thing for another**: To replace primarily means to exchange, to put one thing in the place of another. In Leviticus 27:10, when someone dedicates an animal to the Lord, he cannot "replace" that animal with another, even a better one: the dedicated animal remains dedicated, and one cannot give another in its place.

2. **Transform, alter**: The word can also mean to change the form or nature of something, to upset it. In Psalms 46:3, the earth is "moved," meaning transformed, shaken by the rising waters.

3. **Abandon or renounce**: To replace can mean to give up something or someone, to break a commitment. In Psalms 106:20, Israel "exchanged" its glory (the presence of the true God) for the image of a calf: this is a renunciation, an abandonment of what was sacred for nothingness. Similarly, in Jeremiah 2:11, the people "changed" their glory for what is of no help: this is an act of unfaithfulness.

4. **Transform**: In the so-called "niphal" form (passive form in Hebrew), the word means that something changes, transforms by itself, without direct external action.
H4171.origine: The Hebrew root מוּר expresses the idea of change, transformation. It comes from the image of putting one thing in the place of another, of exchanging. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this word is found to translate concepts of substitution and exchange. The family of this word always carries the fundamental idea: one thing disappears and another takes its place.
H4171.emploi: This verb appears ten times in the Old Testament, notably in the books of the Law and the Psalms. It is mainly found in Leviticus 27, where it concerns animals dedicated to God: it is forbidden to replace or exchange them. In the Psalms and the Prophets, the word takes on a moral tone: Israel "exchanges" its glory for idols (Psalms 106:20, Jeremiah 2:11), which expresses spiritual betrayal. The verb is also used to describe a change of state or situation, like the shaken earth. The forms of the verb vary according to the context: sometimes it is a direct action (one replaces), sometimes it is a transformation (the thing changes).
H4171.portee: This word teaches us that promises and commitments to God are not negotiable: one cannot replace what has been dedicated with something else. More broadly, the idea of exchanging the glory of God for false gods reveals the heart of sin: abandoning the true for the false, the precious for the worthless. It is a call to faithfulness and consistency in our relationship with the Lord.

sens: Fear that grips someone in the face of danger or threat
Respect mixed with dread before a superhuman power
Thing or person that inspires fear
Spectacle or action that provokes astonishment and dread
H4172A.detail:
1. Fear is primarily the concrete fear that a creature feels in the face of danger or an authority that surpasses it. In Genesis 9:2, after the flood, God establishes that animals will have fear of man: it is the natural fear that the human being, as a dominant creature, inspires.
2. This word also designates religious respect, the reverence one feels before God himself or before what comes from Him. It is a feeling that mixes fear and worship, far from being merely negative. In Psalms 76:12, God is called "terrible" to indicate that He inspires this respectful fear.
3. Sometimes the word designates the person or thing itself that inspires this fear. In Deuteronomy 11:25, "the fear of you" means: "the fact that you are feared."
4. It can also describe impressive acts or spectacles that produce dread: in Deuteronomy 4:34 and 26:8, the "wonders of terror" are the miracles that God performed in Egypt, which struck and terrified His adversaries.
H4172A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the impression one receives, a sudden emotion. It is linked to the idea of seeing or perceiving something impressive. In Hebrew, this word is very ancient and is regularly used to express both human fear and reverence towards God, two aspects of the same reaction in the face of what surpasses us.
H4172A.emploi: This word appears eleven times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Pentateuch and the Psalms. In Genesis 9:2, it denotes the fear of animals. In Deuteronomy, it appears several times to speak of the miracles of Egypt or the fear that the peoples will have in the face of Israel. In the Psalms, it directly applies to God: He is called "the terrible God." In Isaiah and Jeremiah, this term describes the fear that God inspires or the wonderful acts He performs. In Malachi, it evokes the respect that children and priests must have for the Lord. The word constantly oscillates between visceral fear and adorable reverence.
H4172A.portee: This word reminds us that the fear of God is not blind servitude, but a deep respect for His power and holiness. It mingles with worship and trust: it is the right attitude before the Creator who infinitely surpasses us. For the believer, this fear gives weight to obedience and prayer.

sens: Intense terror, sudden panic caused by something frightening or powerful
State of deep fear and disarray in the face of an impressive manifestation
Trembler or reverential fear before what inspires respect and fear
H4172B.detail:
1. Dismay is the terror and panic that seize someone in the face of something formidable. In Psalm 9:21, the psalmist asks God to "strike the peoples with dismay" — to seize them with such violent fear that they suddenly realize their fragility and dependence. It is a physical, visceral emotion that paralyzes.
2. The word also evokes this impressive, visible, and powerful manifestation that causes fear — a demonstration of divine strength or power that inspires reverential fear. It is less servile fear than fearful respect, awe in English.
H4172B.origine: The word מוֹרָה (moirah) is a variant or form of the word מוֹרָא (moira, also H4172A). These two forms designate the same reality: fear, fright. They derive from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of what is feared or what makes one tremble. It is a word from the family of the verb יָרֵא (yara) "to fear." The word carries the image of a fear that is evoked by something surpassing and powerful.
H4172B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 9:21, where the psalmist pleads with God to strike the enemy nations with dismay. There, the context is one of a call for divine justice: the dismay that God could inspire is not a simple fear, but an awareness of the divine, a revelation of God's power and justice that transforms the one who receives it. It is a hapax in Psalm 9:21.
H4172B.portee: The word invites the believer to consider the formidable power of God. Biblical dismay is not mere animal terror, but an appropriate reaction to divine holiness and justice. It calls for humility and recognition of our fragility before the One who governs all.

sens: Agricultural instrument consisting of a platform dragged by animals to separate grains from chaff
Cart or work vehicle used in rural and domestic contexts
Figurative image of destructive power at the service of God
H4173.detail:
1. The threshing sled is a traditional instrument of the Middle East: a platform mounted on sleds or wheels, dragged by oxen or horses on the threshing floor, which by its weight and roughness crushes and separates the grains of wheat or barley from the chaff (Isaiah 41:15: "I make you a sharp threshing sled, new, equipped with spikes"). It is an indispensable tool for rural work.
2. In the two historical passages (2 Samuel 24:22 and 1 Chronicles 21:23), the word designates the instrument itself offered to David to burn wood during the sacrifice: Aravna and Ornan generously offer their "carts" with the yoke of oxen, that is, the threshing sled equipped for traction, to serve as fuel.
3. In Isaiah 41:15, the prophet uses the image of the sharp sled crushing mountains to symbolize the destructive power that God will give to Israel over its enemies: the sled becomes a metaphor for the overwhelming force that crushes everything in its path.
H4173.origine: The Hebrew word מוֹרַג (morag) etymologically designates an instrument that "scratches" or "pierces": its root evokes scraping and tearing. The ancient threshing sled indeed had a bottom equipped with stones or metal blades to burst the grain's husk. It is a specialized word in agricultural vocabulary, rarely used outside this context.
H4173.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. Twice in parallel historical accounts (2 Samuel 24:22 and 1 Chronicles 21:23) where it describes a concrete asset: the threshing sled that the landowner generously offers as a sacrifice. Once in Isaiah 41:15 in a poetic and prophetic context, where it becomes a powerful image of devastation: the ordinary agricultural instrument transforms into a cosmic weapon of destruction at the service of God's plan. This progression from the concrete to the figurative shows how the realities of daily work feed biblical imagery.
H4173.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, tools of work and ordinary life become images to speak of God's power. Aravna and Ornan generously offer their work instruments as a sacrifice: it is a lesson in availability and giving. And when God describes Himself in Isaiah as a sled that crushes mountains, it shows us a power that crushes all obstacles to His plan: a force that inspires fear and trust.

sens: Movement downward, slope, hillside of a mountain
Ornament that hangs from a structure, suspended work
Flight or hasty retreat before an enemy
H4174.detail:
1. The descent is primarily the action of going down, or the slope itself — the side of a mountain or hill. In Micah 1:4, the valleys open up "like water flowing down a slope": one sees the terrain sloping down. It is a path that inclines and is taken when descending.
2. The word also refers to works that hang from a structure: in 1 Kings 7:29, on the basin of the temple, there are ornaments "that hung in festoons" — decorations suspended in chains or garlands under the panels.
3. In military accounts (Joshua 7:5 and 10:11), the descent is the terrain that one descends in flight or pursuit: the men of Ai defeat them "at the descent" of Shebarim, meaning on the slope where Israel escapes in disorder. The word then takes on the meaning of a hasty retreat.
H4174.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to lower," "to humble" — hence the idea of something going down. The image is that of a downward movement, natural and inevitable like water flowing. It has also given rise to the words for "hand" (which lowers to act) and "humble."
H4174.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Joshua, Samuel, Kings) and prophetic writings. In Joshua 7:5 and 10:11, it refers to the slopes of the mountains of Canaan where battles take place: it is a terrain well-known from conquest narratives. In 1 Kings 7:29, it takes on an architectural sense: the ornaments of the bronze basin. In Jeremiah 48:5 and Micah 1:4, it is used poetically to describe a mountainous landscape or a judgment that overturns the terrain. The primary meaning remains that of slope or concrete descent.
H4174.portee: This word reminds us that the geography of Canaan was rugged terrain where each battle was also a matter of slope and ground. For the reader, it is an invitation to see how God masters not only the enemy but also the very landscape where events unfold. Slopes are never neutral in the biblical narrative: they slow down or hasten flight.

sens: Rain that falls at the beginning of the rainy season, in autumn-winter
One who teaches, master or instructor
H4175.detail:
1. The early rain is that which falls at the beginning of the wet season in the Holy Land, generally in autumn or early winter, after the dry months of summer. It is essential as it prepares the land for sowing and allows crops to sprout. In Joel 2:23, the Lord promises this early rain as a blessing: "He will give you the rain in its season, the early rain and the latter rain." In Psalms 84:7, it transforms the arid valley of Baca "into a place full of springs."
2. By extension, one who teaches, who instructs. The master is one who gives, who "pours out" his knowledge just as rain enriches the earth. In Proverbs 5:13, the fool refuses to listen to his "teachers"; in Isaiah 30:20, the Lord promises that "your eyes will see your teachers" — the masters will no longer hide, they will guide openly.
H4175.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to throw," "to spread," "to pour out." The same family gives the verb "to teach": just as rain falls and spreads, the teacher pours out his knowledge. The basic image is that of water falling from the sky and enriching: it nourishes, transforms, and brings life. The climate of the Holy Land makes this word particularly rich: the early rain is not just meteorology, it is a divine promise of life and blessing.
H4175.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible. In the provided usages, it first denotes concrete rain: Joel 2:23 and Psalms 84:7 speak of the rain that God grants as a blessing for the harvests. But three occurrences (Job 36:22, Proverbs 5:13, Isaiah 30:20) use the word in the sense of "teacher" or "master." This duality shows how biblical Hebrew understands teaching: as a generous, life-giving action, similar to rain that waters. The teacher who withholds or hides is a misfortune; the one who shows himself and instructs is a blessing.
H4175.portee: This word unites two essential spiritual realities for the people of God: the material abundance that only the Lord can give (the rain), and the richness of divine instruction. It invites us to see our masters and teachers as instruments of the Lord's blessing, and to recognize that all wisdom, all true instruction, comes from God alone as a free gift. Rejecting the teaching received from God is to reject his life-giving rain.

sens: Place name or natural sanctuary marked by an oak near Shechem
H4176G.detail: 1. The name refers to an oak or grove of oaks located near Shechem, in the land of Canaan. It is an important geographical landmark: Abram arrives there when entering the promised land for the first time (Genesis 12:6), and Deuteronomy precisely locates it between the Jordan and the mountains of Ebal and Gerizim (Deuteronomy 11:30). The oak was a sacred tree in antiquity, often associated with the divine presence and decisive encounters; thus, this place carries symbolic and religious significance.
H4176G.origine: The Hebrew name מוֹרֶה (moreh) literally means "one who teaches" or "master" — it comes from the root יָרָה (yarah), which means "to teach" or "to show." Why does an oak bear this name? Probably because the oak, by its majesty and longevity, was seen as a manifestation of God's wisdom, a silent "teacher" that "teaches" through its presence. The same place appears in the Old Testament as a sacred landmark related to divine revelation.
H4176G.emploi: Moreh appears only twice in the Bible, always referring to the same place: the oak (or grove of oaks) near Shechem. In Genesis 12:6, Abram passes by it upon his entry into Canaan, a key moment when God appears to him and confirms the promise of the land. In Deuteronomy 11:30, Moreh serves as a topographical marker to locate the mountains of Ebal and Gerizim, where Israel must pronounce the blessings and curses of the Covenant. In both cases, the place is associated with the promised land and God's Covenant with his people.
H4176G.portee: Moreh reminds us that geographical locations in biblical history are not neutral: it is upon arriving at this oak that the patriarch Abram receives the divine promise. The reader sees that God sanctifies the places where he reveals himself and guides his people toward the promised inheritance. This name of "teaching" invites us to recognize that God "teaches" through the events and places of his history with his people.

sens: A hill located in the valley of Jezreel
H4176H.detail: Moreh is the name of a hill that rises in the valley of Jezreel, a fertile region in northern Israel. It is the place where the Midianites had set up their camp when Gideon attacked them with his three hundred men (Judges 7:1). This hill served as an important geographical landmark for locating military positions in this famous battle.
H4176H.origine: The Hebrew word moreh (מוֹרֶה) literally means "one who teaches" or "master." The name of this hill may evoke an ancient religious function or a characteristic of the mountain itself, although the biblical text does not explain this. It is a proper geographical name passed down through ancient tradition.
H4176H.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 7:1, to designate the position of the Midianite enemy camp. The text specifies that this camp was located "to the north of Gideon, toward the hill of Moreh," which shows that the name served to identify a place known to the Israelite readers of the time. This contextual mention helps to understand the unfolding of the battle where Gideon achieved a miraculous victory over the Midianites despite his numerical inferiority.

sens: Cutting instrument used to shave hair or beard
Symbol of the status of a nazirite, one who vows to remain consecrated to God
H4177.detail:
1. The razor is a cutting instrument used for shaving. It is the physical object itself, as it is used daily for personal hygiene.

2. In the Bible, "the razor shall not pass over his head" means that a person will never be shaved: it is the visible and permanent sign of the nazirite vow, one who is wholly dedicated to God. Samson, born a nazirite, was never to cut his hair (Judges 13:5). When he broke this vow by having his hair cut, he lost his strength and his consecration (Judges 16:17). This absence of shaving was therefore much more than a mere matter of appearance: it publicly manifested the sacred covenant with God.
H4177.origine: The Hebrew word *mo.rah* comes from the root meaning "to cut" or "to shave." It is a concrete word, directly designating the tool. It does not have a particularly common equivalent in related biblical words, but the image is clear: it is what cuts, what shaves hair.
H4177.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the context of the nazirite vow. It is found in the story of Samson (Judges 13:5 and 16:17) and in the story of Hannah, who dedicates her son Samuel to God (1 Samuel 1:11). In each case, it emphasizes that the consecrated person must never be shaved: this is an essential condition of the vow. The razor is therefore never used to describe an ordinary act of grooming, but only to mark this commitment to God.
H4177.portee: For the believing reader, the razor in these verses reveals what it truly means to be consecrated to God: it is a public and visible position, not hidden. The long hair of the nazirites spoke to the entire community of Israel. This teaches that faithfulness to God must manifest outwardly, through our concrete and observable choices, and that breaking it has real consequences.

sens: mountain near Jerusalem where Abraham offered Isaac as a sacrifice
place where Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem
H4179.detail:
1. Moriah is the mountain in the land of Canaan where God commanded Abraham to offer his only son Isaac as a sacrifice. This is a foundational event of biblical faith: Abraham obeys God and goes to Moriah with Isaac, ready to accomplish what seemed impossible (Genesis 22:2).

2. Centuries later, the same mountain, Moriah in Jerusalem, became the site where King Solomon built the temple, the house of God at the heart of the nation of Israel. This place thus held a particular sacredness in the history of Israel (2 Chronicles 3:1).
H4179.origine: The name Moriah literally means "chosen by the Lord" or "God will see." It carries the idea that this place was designated by God Himself. It is a proper Hebrew name that expresses the holiness of the place and the divine character of its selection for decisive events in the history of salvation.
H4179.emploi: Moriah appears twice in the Bible translated by Segond: first in Genesis 22:2, where God indicates to Abraham the mountain of Moriah as the place for Isaac's sacrifice, one of the key moments of biblical faith; then in 2 Chronicles 3:1, where it is identified as the mountain in Jerusalem where Solomon built the temple. These two occurrences reveal that the same place bears the dual mark of personal faith sacrifice and the presence of the temple, the religious center of Israel.
H4179.portee: Moriah symbolizes for the believer the place where faith is manifested through absolute obedience (the sacrifice of Isaac) and where God establishes His dwelling among His people (the temple). This name reminds us that God "sees" and "chooses," and that the places where He manifests are destined to become places of encounter between the human and the divine.

sens: What one possesses, what one owns
Plan, project that one forms and carries within oneself
Territory, domain that one occupies and controls
H4180.detail:
1. The primary meaning is material possession: what one holds, has acquired, or inherited. In Job 17:11, Job speaks of his "plans" (literally: what he intended to possess, what he wanted to accomplish), which illness and suffering have destroyed — this is all he had in view, his concrete hopes.
2. By extension, the word designates a project, an intention, a plan that one forms. It is something one "holds" mentally, carries in one's heart, and hopes to realize.
3. In Obadiah 1:17, "recovering one's possessions" means reconquering a territory, reclaiming what once belonged to Jacob. The word also refers to a domain, a region that one occupies and controls. In Isaiah 14:23, Babylon will become the "den" of the hedgehog — an uninhabited place, reduced to ruin where only wild animals live.
H4180.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to possess" or "to inherit." It is formed to designate what is possessed, held, or inherited. The family of the word connects it to the idea of appropriation and control: one "holds" something, making it one's own. The basic image is that of seizing and retaining.
H4180.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 17:11, it describes the plans and hopes that Job carried in his heart before his catastrophe. In Isaiah 14:23, it designates a place, reduced to a den for animals after destruction. In Obadiah 1:17, it refers to the territory that God's people will reclaim after exile. The context shows that the word shifts from a concrete sense (what one holds materially or territorially) to a more abstract sense (what one conceives mentally as one's own, what one hopes to have or do).
H4180.portee: This word reminds us that our plans and projects never truly belong to us — only God disposes of them. It also invites the reader to meditate on the difference between what we think we possess and what eludes us, and on the restoration that God offers to His people, beyond exile and ruin.

sens: What one possesses, what belongs to us
A property, a land that one holds and can transmit
The right to enjoy and use something
The inheritance received from the fathers
H4181.detail: 1. The word first designates what one possesses concretely: a good, a property. When God says to Israel, "I will give it to you as a possession" (Exodus 6:8), He speaks of the land of Canaan as a territory that will become their own, which God grants to them. 2. It is also a good that can be transmitted to one's heirs, a heritage that passes from one generation to another. Abraham "inherited the land" (Ezekiel 33:24), and his descendants receive possession of it in turn. 3. Possession implies a right: it is the ability to enjoy something and use it according to one's will. When Israel's enemies threaten it, God affirms that this land remains Israel's possession, not that of its aggressors (Ezekiel 25:10). 4. By extension, the word can qualify the inheritance in a figurative sense: the Law that Moses gave to Israel is called "inheritance" (Deuteronomy 33:4), a spiritual good transmitted by the Lord.
H4181.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root יָרַשׁ (yarash), which means "to inherit," "to take possession of," "to chase to appropriate." מוֹרָשָׁה (morashah) is the feminine noun derived from the same root. The basic image is that of something transmitted, received as an inheritance, and over which one becomes master in place of the previous occupant.
H4181.emploi: This word appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in Ezekiel and once in Exodus and Deuteronomy. In Exodus 6:8, it designates the Promised Land that God promises to give to Israel. In Deuteronomy 33:4, it qualifies the Law itself as an inheritance. But it is especially in Ezekiel (chapters 11, 25, 33, 36) that it recurs: the prophet uses it to affirm that the land of Israel remains the possession of the people of Israel despite invasions and threats from enemies (Moab, Ammon, and others). The meaning remains stable: a good that one holds, that can be transmitted, and over which one has a confirmed right.
H4181.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that God does not give lightly: He promises a possession, stability, and security in what He grants to His people. For Israel, it was the land; for the believer today, it is the assurance that God solidifies our spiritual goods — salvation, new life in Christ — and does not take them back. It is a term that speaks of acquired rights and durability, not of borrowing or precariousness.

sens: City or locality in Judah, probably near Gath
Place of origin of the prophet Micah
H4182.detail: Moresheth-Gath is a small city or locality in Judah, located in the region of Gath, in southern Israel. Its name literally means "possession of Gath," indicating its geographical or administrative link to Gath, an important city of the Philistines. It is apparently the place from which the prophet Micah came, as indicated in Micah 1:14, where God announces that the people must forsake this city due to the divine judgment that is coming upon the region.
H4182.origine: The name Moresheth-Gath is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Moresheth" means "possession" or "heritage," and "Gath" is the name of a major Philistine city. Thus, the locality bears a name that indicates its association with Gath. Micah is referred to as "Micah of Moresheth" in reference to this city, which was a common way to identify prophets by their place of origin.
H4182.emploi: Moresheth-Gath appears only once in the Bible, in Micah 1:14. In this verse, God pronounces judgment on the cities of Judah, including Moresheth-Gath, announcing that the people must forsake this possession. This context of divine judgment on the cities of the region reflects the threats of destruction looming over Judah during the time of the prophet Micah, around the 8th century B.C.

sens: City or locality in Judah in antiquity
Homeland of the prophet Micah
H4183.detail: Moresheth is a small town in the region of Judah, probably located in the lowlands of the southwest. The prophet Micah was from there — he was called "Micah of Moresheth" (Micah 1:1) — and it is from there that he exercised his ministry in the 8th century B.C., under the kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah.
H4183.origine: The name Moresheth means "possession" (Hebrew morasha) and is added to "Gath," the famous Philistine city, suggesting that this locality was linked to the region of Gath. It is an ordinary geographical place, mentioned only as a reference point to identify the prophet Micah.
H4183.emploi: Moresheth appears twice in the Bible, exclusively to designate the homeland of Micah. In Micah 1:1, it is mentioned as the place from which the prophet receives the word of God during the time of three kings of Judah. In Jeremiah 26:18, it is recalled in a historical citation: the elders of Judah invoke the words that Micah of Moresheth spoke during the reign of Hezekiah, words that foretold the destruction of Jerusalem. These two references emphasize the connection between authentic prophecy and its geographical origin.
H4183.portee: For the Christian reader, Moresheth reminds us that God chooses His prophets from ordinary places, cities without prestige, and entrusts His word to simple men. Micah's reputation rests not on his prestigious origin, but on the authenticity and power of his message. This invites respect for the word of God not according to human appearances, but according to His faithfulness.

sens: To make physical contact with something or someone
To perceive by the sense of touch
To feel in order to recognize or verify
H4184.detail:
1. To touch means to establish direct physical contact with someone or something. It is the action of putting one's hand or body in contact with an object or person. Isaac says to Jacob: "Come near, that I may touch you, my son" (Genesis 27:21), he wants to feel his son to verify his identity by touch.

2. Touching is also the ability to perceive through the hands or skin, the sense that allows one to feel material, texture, temperature. This is why idols have no sense of touch: "They have hands but do not touch" (Psalms 115:7) — their hands cannot perceive anything.

3. To touch can mean to feel deliberately in order to recognize, examine, or verify something. Samson asks the young man: "Let me go, that I may touch the pillars" (Judges 16:26), he wants to feel the pillars to locate exactly where to strike.
H4184.origine: The Hebrew word mush comes from a simple root that denotes the action of feeling or touching. In Hebrew, touching is an active verb: the one who touches acts upon what he touches. This verb is infrequent in the Bible; when it appears, it is always in situations where the touch has a specific intention: to verify, recognize, feel in order to act.
H4184.emploi: The verb mush appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis, Isaac, who has become blind, wants to touch Jacob to verify who he really is. In Judges, blind Samson also asks to touch the pillars to locate his target before an act of vengeance. In Psalms, the psalmist affirms that idols have hands but do not touch anything, highlighting their radical impotence. The word designates each time a deliberate action, not a mere passive contact.
H4184.portee: Touching in the Bible is never trivial: it is an act of investigation, recognition, verification. Isaac touches to identify, Samson to prepare an act of power. This word reminds us that in the biblical experience, the body is not separate from knowledge — one also knows through hands and skin. For believers, this suggests that faith is not purely intellectual, but engages our senses and our bodies in relation to God and the world.

sens: To move away, to withdraw from a place
To take away, to remove something or someone from a place
To cease, to not continue an action
To remain absent, to not manifest oneself
H4185.detail:
1. To move away, to withdraw: the subject moves and leaves a place. The pillar of cloud that guides Israel "did not withdraw" from before the people (Exodus 13:22), it remained constantly present.
2. To take away, to remove: the subject actively removes something or someone. This is the sense of the command to Joshua: "This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth" (Joshua 1:8), meaning it should remain constantly with you, do not set it aside.
3. To cease, to not continue: the action or state stops or disappears. Fraud "does not depart" from the places of the city (Psalms 55:12) — it persists constantly there. Likewise, the flourishing tree "does not cease to bear fruit" (Jeremiah 17:8), it bears without interruption.
4. To remain absent, to not manifest oneself: a reality or help does not present itself. The idol "does not move from its place" and "does not respond" to the one who pleads with it (Isaiah 46:7) — it is powerless and mute.
H4185.origine: The Hebrew verb mush fundamentally means "to leave, to let go." It evokes the idea of separation or rupture — something or someone that detaches. The context determines whether it is the subject itself that departs, or if it is an external force that removes. In Hebrew, this verb mainly appears in historical and poetic narratives to express absence, continuity, or interruption.
H4185.emploi: The verb mush appears 19 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical and prophetic books. In Exodus 13:22, it describes the constant divine presence (the cloud does not depart). In Joshua 1:8 and Jeremiah 17:8, it expresses the persistence of an attitude or blessing (not to depart, not to cease). Its most intense uses are found in Isaiah (Isaiah 46:7; 54:10; 59:21), where it emphasizes God's unwavering commitment to His people: His goodness "will not depart" (Isaiah 54:10). Elsewhere, it describes evil that "does not cease" to persist (Nahum 3:1; Psalms 55:12), or destruction that falls upon someone (Micah 2:3-4).
H4185.portee: This verb helps to understand how the Bible speaks of God's faithfulness: His promises and protection "do not depart" from the believer, they remain anchored. Conversely, it also shows how sin persists when one does not turn away from it. It is a word of lasting commitment — whether it is God's commitment to His people, or the believer's duty to keep the Word of God constantly present in their life (Joshua 1:8).

sens: The seat where someone sits, the chair or bench occupied
The place assigned at a table or in assembly
The place where one lives, the house or inhabited territory
The collective inhabitants of a region, those who dwell somewhere
The official or sacred residence, the sanctuary
H4186.detail:
1. The seat itself is the piece of furniture on which one sits: in 1 Samuel 20:25, King Saul sat "on his seat" as usual, and it is noted that David's place, normally occupied, remained empty. This is the most concrete and material sense of the word.

2. By extension, the place or position that someone occupies in an assembly or at a table: in 2 Chronicles 9:4, we see the "dwelling" of the king's servants, meaning their rank and function before him, which shows us how they were organized and served.

3. The main place of habitation, the home: in Psalms 132:13, the Lord chose Zion for His "dwelling," meaning to make His presence reside there. This sense also includes the ordinary dwellings of humans.

4. The collective inhabitants of a place or the people who dwell there: in Genesis 10:30, it refers to the territory where certain peoples lived; in Leviticus 3:17, "the places where you will dwell" refers to the regions populated by the Israelites, with the idea of the populations that occupy them.

5. The sanctuary or divine residence: Psalms 132:13 uses it to speak of the place that God chooses, suggesting not only a physical space but the sacred dwelling of God among His people.
H4186.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to sit" or "to dwell." It is a noun derived from a very common verb in Hebrew, which initially designated the action of sitting (hence "seat"), then by extension the place where one regularly sits, and then the home and habitat. The family of the word includes the general idea of "residence" or "place of parking" — a place where one establishes oneself.
H4186.emploi: The word appears 43 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books, the laws of Leviticus, and the Psalms. It designates sometimes a material seat (1 Samuel 20:25), sometimes a dwelling or home (Psalms 132:13), sometimes an inhabited region (Genesis 10:30, Leviticus 3:17). In the legislative texts of Leviticus, it often recurs in the expression "in all the places where you will dwell" to signify the regions of Israel. In the prophets, particularly Ezekiel, it designates places of human or divine residence. The meaning varies according to the context: physical and concrete (the seat of a king), geographical (the inhabited lands), or theological (the dwelling of God).
H4186.portee: This word reminds us that dwelling, rest, and stable presence are important in both human and divine life. When the psalmist says that God chose Zion for His dwelling, it means that God is not distant but establishes a lasting presence among His people. For the reader, it is an invitation to see that God desires to dwell near us, just as we seek a safe and stable place to reside. The word also emphasizes the biblical idea that the presence of God transforms a simple place into a sanctuary.

sens: Son of Merari, in the genealogy of the Levites
Ancestor of a branch of the tribe of Levi
Founder of the family of the Mushites
H4187.detail:
1. Mushi is a character from the Old Testament, son of Merari and grandson of Kohath. He appears in the genealogical records of Israel as one of the two main branches of the family of Merari (the other being his brother Mahli). He lived during the time of Egypt and the desert, after the exodus from Egypt.

2. Mushi is the father of Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth, thus founding a new generation of Levites. His family branch perpetuates the lineage of the descendants of Kohath and Levi, one of the ancestors of the twelve tribes of Israel. Several of his descendants are mentioned as performing religious functions in the temple (1 Chronicles 23:23).

3. The Mushites (descendants of Mushi) form a distinct Levitical family, recognized alongside the other branches of the Levites in the organization of worship and service of the tabernacle. They occupy a specific place in the distribution of tasks and dwellings among the Levites.
H4187.origine: The name Mushi means "he who yields" or "he who delivers," evoking an image of submission or surrender. It belongs to the genealogy of the Levites, the tribe dedicated to serving God in Israelite worship. Mushi is an essential link in the genealogical chain that traces back to Levi, one of Jacob's sons, and structures the religious organization of Israel.
H4187.emploi: Mushi is mentioned eight times in the biblical texts, exclusively in genealogical lists and in records of Levitical organization. He first appears in Exodus 6:19, where his lineage is established: son of Merari, brother of Mahli. This passage lays the foundation for his place in the tribal structure. In Numbers 3:20, he is again cited in the context of the census of the Levites and the organization of their families. The most detailed mentions are found in 1 Chronicles, particularly in chapters 6, 23, and 24, which enumerate not only Mushi but also his three sons (Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth), showing how his family branch developed and organized itself in the service of the temple in Jerusalem.
H4187.portee: Mushi reminds us that every human life is part of a larger genealogical story, a plan of God that extends from generation to generation. His name, which evokes submission, illustrates how the tribe of Levi placed itself in the service of the Lord, not by constraint but by calling. Seeing how Mushi and his descendants served faithfully through the ages encourages the believer to recognize their own place in God's eternal project.

sens: Descendant of Mushi, son of Merari and grandson of Levi
Member of the Levitical family of the Mushites
H4188.detail:
1. Mushi is primarily a man, son of Merari (who was the son of Levi) and brother of Mahli. He lived during the time of Egypt and the desert, and is first mentioned in Exodus 6:19. He is an ancestor of the Levitical clan that will bear his name.
2. The Mushites are the descendants of this ancestor Mushi. They form an officially recognized Levitical family in the census of the tribes of Israel. In Numbers 3:33, they are listed among the families of the Merarites, alongside the family of Mahli. In Numbers 26:58, during a new census, the Mushites appear again in the list of Levitical families.
H4188.origine: The name Mushi comes from a Hebrew root evoking the idea of "to yield" or "to render." It designates both the eponymous ancestor (the founder) of the family and all his descendants. Mushi was the son of Merari, himself a direct son of Levi, which places the Mushites in the oldest and most noble genealogy of the Levites.
H4188.emploi: The word appears twice in the Segond 1910: first in Numbers 3:33 and in Numbers 26:58. Each time it refers to an official census of the Levitical families. The Mushites are always associated with the Merarites (from whom they descend) and listed among the great priestly families of Israel. This administrative and religious census underscores the importance of the Mushites in the organization of worship and service of the tabernacle.
H4188.portee: The Mushites remind the people of Israel that the service of God is part of a respectable and orderly genealogy. They also illustrate how God organizes His people by families and lineages, each having its place and function. The name of this humble yet established clan invites the believer to see themselves as part of a living spiritual lineage.

sens: rope, braided or knotted string
set of strings
link, tie
that which holds, that which binds
H4189.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a rope or string, that is, a braided or knotted object capable of binding and holding. This is the physical, concrete sense: a twisted or braided material used to assemble, attach, or transport.
2. It can also refer to a set or system of strings — a rigging, a complex ligature — like that which would hold the stars together. In Job 38:31, God asks Job if he can "loosen the cords of Orion": the image is that of the invisible ties that would hold the constellations of Orion in place.
3. Figuratively, the word takes on the meaning of a link or tie in a broad sense — that which connects, that which unites, that which assembles things.
4. By extension, it symbolizes that which holds, masters, or controls — the idea that something is maintained, governed, held together by a force or authority.
H4189.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to pull, to draw, to extend." This image of tension and pulling is found in several words of the same family. The cordage is what is extended, what is pulled to bind and hold together. It is a worked, shaped material intended to assemble and control.
H4189.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 38:31. God speaks to Job, who has questioned His justice and wisdom, and poses a series of questions about creation and the governance of the universe. Among these questions is this one: can he bind the Pleiades or loosen the cords of Orion? The usage is highly poetic and cosmic. The word symbolizes the invisible ties that maintain the order of the heavens, the constellations in their place. It is a way of saying: only God masters the structure and cohesion of the universe.
H4189.portee: This image of cosmic cordage reminds the believer that only God governs the universe in its smallest details — even the distant and unchanging stars obey a logic and order that surpass our understanding. It invites humility before divine wisdom and power, and to recognize that we do not control the world. For the believing reader, it is an invitation to trust the One who holds everything together.

sens: The act of saving someone, pulling them from danger
The act of escaping death or a deadly threat
The helpful aid that God provides to His people
H4190.detail:
1. Deliverance is the act of saving someone who is in peril or captivity. It is intervening to free them and bring them to safety. In Psalms 68:21, God is called "the God of deliverances": He is the one who acts to save His people from the traps and threats that surround them.

2. More specifically, it often involves escaping death or destruction. The psalmist says that the Lord "can guarantee us from death": it is a deliverance from the ultimate peril. God has the power to snatch His people from death itself.

3. On a spiritual level, deliverance is the work of salvation that God accomplishes. It is not a human or accidental deliverance, but one that comes from the hand of God Himself, who personally commits to saving His own.
H4190.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "yasha" which means "to save" or "to be wide, spacious." The basic idea is that of space, of freedom: one is saved when moving from narrowness (captivity, the trap) to space (freedom). The form "moshaa" carries the idea of a completed action, an act of salvation that has been realized. This word belongs to the same family as "Yéshoua" (Jesus), which literally means "the Lord saves."
H4190.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 68:21, where it is in the plural: "deliverances." The psalmist acknowledges that God is characterized not by a single deliverance, but by a series of saving acts toward His people. By using the plural, the text emphasizes that God is accustomed to saving, that His repeated intervention is His distinctive mark. It is a rare but powerful word that recapitulates the entire history of salvation: God has always been the one who delivers.
H4190.portee: For the believer, recognizing God as "the God of deliverances" means trusting that He intervenes to save us from real threats — spiritual, moral, or physical — that weigh upon us. It is also a reminder that salvation is not our work, but that of God alone. This word invites us to celebrate all the acts of rescue that God has accomplished and to await with assurance His protection in the future.

sens: To cease living, to breathe one's last
To be put to death, executed by sentence
To perish, to disappear (referring to a people, a nation)
To die prematurely due to a lack of wisdom or prudence
H4191.detail:
1. To cease living naturally: this is the most basic sense, that of the end of earthly life. Adam learns in Genesis 2:17 that he "will die" the day he eats the forbidden fruit. The patriarchs die: Abraham "died... satisfied with days" (Genesis 25:8), Noah and his descendants (Genesis 5:5,8,11...).
2. To be put to death, executed according to the law: this is capital punishment. Whoever profanes the Sabbath will be "punished with death" (Exodus 31:14). Both the adulterer and the adulteress "shall surely be put to death" according to Deuteronomy 22:22.
3. To perish or disappear as a people or nation: when Saul and his sons died in battle, Israel fled because the king and his army had "perished" (1 Samuel 31:7).
4. To die before one's time, prematurely, often as a consequence of sin or carelessness: Proverbs 19:16 warns that "he who does not take heed to his way will die," meaning he will suffer an early death due to a lack of wisdom.
H4191.origine: The Hebrew verb mut literally means "to cease to live." It expresses the irreversible cessation of life. The root describes a passive state: one undergoes death rather than accomplishes it. In Hebrew, it conjugates in several forms (Qal = simple form, Polel = intensive, Hiphil = causative "to cause to die"), which nuance the meaning: to die, to kill, to put to death. It is a fundamental word in the Old Testament that appears nearly 700 times.
H4191.emploi: This verb appears about 700 times in the Old Testament. It is first encountered at the heart of the creation narrative (Genesis 2-3), where God warns Adam of death as a consequence of sin. It then becomes omnipresent: natural death of the patriarchs (Genesis 5, 25, 35), judicial death (Exodus 31:14), death in battle (1 Samuel 31:7), death by famine (2 Kings 7:4). The context varies: sometimes it is an inevitable and dignified event ("to die satisfied with days"), sometimes a punishment ("you shall surely die"), sometimes an immediate peril. In Proverbs, dying prematurely illustrates the consequences of sin or folly. This word carries an increasingly theological significance: death is not natural; it is linked to sin and divine justice.
H4191.portee: This word invites the reader to grasp the seriousness of sin and its ultimate consequence: death. It also reveals that life is not a guaranteed possession, but a gift from God subject to His laws. For the believer of the Old Testament, understanding the "you shall die" of Genesis 2:17 is to hear the call to obedience and the fear of God. For the New Testament reader who knows the Gospel, this word resonates with the hope of resurrection in Christ: physical death no longer has the final word.

sens: Male child in relation to his parents
In a broader sense, descendant or family member
A person who has a relationship of dependence or belonging to someone else
H4192.detail: 1. Male child: this is the most direct meaning of the word. In the Bible, the son is the heir and bearer of his father's name — a very important reality in Hebrew culture. 2. Descendant or family member: the word expands to refer not only to the direct child but to any descendant. 3. In the sense of a relationship of belonging: one who depends on someone or is their disciple is called a 'son' — for example, the 'sons of the prophets' are the disciples of prophets. The title found in Psalms 9:1, 'To the chief musician. On Muth-labben,' is a riddle: perhaps the name of a melody or a musical note, or maybe an expression that we no longer understand today.
H4192.origine: The Hebrew word לַבֵּן (labben) is formed from the preposition לְ ('for, towards') and the noun בֵּן (ben), which literally means 'son'. This word ben is one of the most fundamental realities of the Hebrew language: it appears hundreds of times in the Bible to express sonship, inheritance, and belonging. The family was the center of Israelite life, and the son held an honored place.
H4192.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond translations, in Psalms 9:1, in the title of the psalm: 'To the chief musician. On Muth-labben.' This is likely a musical indication or the title of a melody known at the time of David, the exact meaning of which escapes us today. This occurrence shows how ancient titles of psalms can contain words whose historical or musical context we no longer grasp.
H4192.portee: This word reminds us of the importance that the Bible places on the parental relationship and transmission. The son is not simply an individual, but a link in the chain of generations. For the Christian faith, the title 'Son of God' given to Jesus takes up this logic: it expresses both an intimate relationship and a spiritual inheritance. Reflecting on the meaning of 'son' helps to understand the biblical genealogies and the promises made to the descendants of Abraham.

sens: the cessation of physical life
the ultimate punishment, capital punishment
H4193.detail:
1. Death is the cessation of life in the body, the end of earthly existence. It is the most direct Aramaic word to name this ultimate reality of the human condition.
2. Here, in Ezra 7:26, death specifically refers to the capital punishment pronounced by the king's justice against one who transgresses God's law: it is a death sentence, among other possible punishments (banishment, fine, imprisonment).
H4193.origine: This Aramaic word מוֹת (mot) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word מָוֶת (mawèt, H4194), which shares the same root and fundamental meaning. It is a simple and direct word, used since the early times of the Bible to name the irreversible reality of death. In Aramaic, it retains exactly this meaning and gravity.
H4193.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 7:26. It is found in the decree that King Artaxerxes addresses to Ezra regarding the administration of justice according to God's law and the king's law in Judah. There, death is listed as one of the four possible penalties (alongside banishment, fine, and imprisonment) for anyone who does not respect the laws in force. It thus represents the most severe punishment, reserved for the most serious offenses.
H4193.portee: This passage reminds us that death is not just a natural inevitability: it can also be a consequence of transgression. For the believer, this underscores the importance of obedience to God's law and the authority that God himself grants to his representatives to maintain order and justice. It is also an invitation to take our choices and responsibilities seriously in light of God's Word.

sens: Cessation of life, end of the existence of a person or a living being.
Action of dying, process of death.
Capital punishment, judicial execution.
State of death, condition or place of the dead.
Power or personification of death.
Destruction, ruin, end (in a figurative sense).
H4194.detail:
1. Death is the cessation of life: it is what inevitably happens to every living being. In Genesis 27:2, a very old father says, 'I do not know if I will see much longer' — he senses death approaching and wants to give his last instructions.
2. To die is to go through the process of death. Genesis 21:16 shows a mother crying, 'Let me not see the death of my child!' — she fears seeing him expire.
3. Death can also be a legal punishment: a death sentence. Deuteronomy 21:22 speaks of a 'criminal sentenced to death.'
4. The state of death is also the abode of the dead, the place where the deceased go. Psalms 6:6 says 'in death' to refer to the place or state where the dead no longer praise God.
5. Sometimes the Bible speaks of death as a power, almost personified. Isaiah 28:18 says, 'Your covenant with death will be annulled' — death appears there as a power with which one can negotiate, like an enemy.
6. Figuratively, death can mean ruin or the end of something: losing one's moral life, freedom, or honor.
H4194.origine: The Hebrew word māvet comes from a root that simply expresses the idea of no longer being, of disappearing. It is a fundamental word in Hebrew, universal to all Semitic peoples: it is found in Aramaic (mot), in Arabic (mawt). It has no scholarly etymology — it is a primitive word, a universal human reality designated by simple and ancient sounds in Middle Eastern languages.
H4194.emploi: The word māvet appears 151 times in the Hebrew Bible, which shows its omnipresence. It is found from Genesis onward and in all historical, poetic, and prophetic books. It primarily denotes the raw fact of dying: Joshua 1:1 speaks of 'the death of Moses' as a historical event. But it also covers nuances: death as punishment (Deuteronomy 21:22, where a law concerns 'a criminal sentenced to death'), death as a feared power (Psalms 18:5-6, where the 'cords of death' or the 'snares of the grave' surround the righteous), or death as a desire to escape suffering (Job 3:21, where the unfortunate wishes for death). The context shifts the meaning between a simple natural death and a violent death, between physical reality and spiritual force.
H4194.portee: Death is an unavoidable reality that the Bible does not hide. It invites the believer to reflect: is it an absolute end or a passage? Understanding how the Bible speaks of death — with gravity, but also with hope in God — helps the Christian not to flee from it, but to face it with confidence. For an evangelical, it is also the starting point of the Gospel: the death of Christ conquers death and promises a resurrection.

sens: Wealth and produce resulting from work
Advantage, superiority of one thing over another
H4195.detail:
1. The word designates the concrete and generous result of work: what accumulates, what emerges as surplus. In Proverbs 14:23, "all labor brings abundance" expresses how effort produces wealth and provision. It is the image of a generous harvest, a tangible material gain that work accumulates.
2. More broadly, it refers to the advantage or superiority of one thing compared to another. In Ecclesiastes 3:19, the author asserts that "the superiority of man over the beast is nothing": here the word weighs what could tip the balance one way or another. It conveys the idea of surplus, excess, of what places one person or situation above another.
H4195.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to remain, to subsist, to exceed." The central idea is that of what "remains" after expenditure, what "surpasses" or "exceeds." This image of surplus or excess unites all usages: abundance is what remains when work has done its job; superiority is what exceeds in one compared to another.
H4195.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the wisdom books. Two occurrences (Proverbs 14:23 and 21:5) are in the context of work and diligence: work produces abundance, while laziness leads to want. A third occurrence (Ecclesiastes 3:19) uses it in a pessimistic reflection on the human condition: in the face of death, no true superiority distinguishes man from animal. The word thus appears in contexts of comparison: between work and idleness, between man and beast.
H4195.portee: This word invites the reader to consider the concrete fruits of their engagement in honest work, and not to confuse material abundance with true superiority or lasting value. Ecclesiastes reminds us that no earthly accumulation changes what we are before death. However, Proverbs affirms that diligent work bears true fruit and deserves to be pursued—not out of illusion, but as an expression of wisdom.

sens: Structure of stone or wood where sacrifices were offered to God
Element of the worship of the Lord, place of encounter between God and His people
Symbol of devotion and obedience to God
H4196.detail:
1. The altar is primarily a material structure: a table or mound where offerings are presented. Noah built an altar after the flood and offered burnt offerings there (Genesis 8:20), while Exodus precisely describes its construction and dimensions (Exodus 27:1).
2. It is also the heart of Israelite worship. Sacrifices are poured or burned there: blood is placed on the horns of the altar (Leviticus 9:9), and grain offerings are presented there (Leviticus 2:2). The altar is sacred, set apart from the profane, and it is where relationships between God and His people are established.
3. Symbolically, the altar represents consecration and obedience: building an altar is to acknowledge God's lordship over one's life and to place one's possessions, family, and will in the hands of the Lord, as Noah and Abraham did.
H4196.origine: The Hebrew word miz.be.ach comes from a root meaning "to slaughter" or "to sacrifice," which recalls the primary function of the altar: the place where sacrificial animals are slaughtered. The word thus evokes the act of sacrifice that defines it. This root appears in other forms designating worship and offering in Israel.
H4196.emploi: The altar appears 338 times in the Old Testament, very often in Exodus and Leviticus where the prescriptions for worship are given. Before the construction of the Tabernacle, the patriarchs built altars during divine revelations: Abraham raised several (Genesis 12:7, 12:8, 13:4), as did Isaac (Genesis 26:25) and Jacob (Genesis 35:1). Exodus describes the golden altar for incense (Exodus 30:1) and the bronze altar for burnt offerings (Exodus 38:1). Leviticus details its use: pouring of blood, presentation of offerings, consecration. It is a technical term of liturgical vocabulary, but also a fundamental religious act for any believer who acknowledges God's Lordship.
H4196.portee: The altar reminds us that biblical faith is not only internal: it is expressed through concrete acts of devotion and sacrifice. For a believer today, the altar invites one to place their life, possessions, and decisions in the hands of the Lord, like Abraham offering what he holds most dear. It is a powerful symbol of submission to God and communion with Him.

sens: wine mixed with other ingredients
refined and flavored drink
blend offered to guests at a feast
H4197.detail:
1. The word designates carefully prepared wine, to which spices, honey, aromatic herbs, or other wines are added to enhance its taste and fragrance. It is a luxury drink, reserved for solemn occasions or refined hospitality. In Song of Solomon 7:3, the beloved is compared to a breast "where the perfumed wine is not lacking," an image of sweetness and delicate allure.
2. This type of mixed wine symbolizes refinement and care in preparation, unlike ordinary wine. It is an intentionally crafted drink that honors the hosts.
H4197.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to mix." It expresses the idea of combining several elements to create something new and improved. In biblical culture, preparing a mixed wine was an art and a mark of generosity towards guests.
H4197.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 7:3, where it describes an aromatic and refined wine. The poetic context—a laudatory description of the beloved's body—highlights the precious and delightful nature of this drink. The image of mixed wine reinforces the impression of sweetness, fragrance, and sensual allure in this passage of mutual praise.
H4197.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, the concrete details of daily life—here the preparation of a drink—often serve to express deep feelings and spiritual values. The notion of skillful mixing also suggests that divine beauty and goodness can result from a delicate harmony between several elements.

sens: To be exhausted, emptied of strength or content
To lose all vitality, to wither
To be consumed, annihilated
H4198.detail:
1. The word evokes the image of something that has completely emptied itself of what kept it alive or functional—like a spring that dries up or a body that loses its strength. In Deuteronomy 32:24, the unfaithful Israelites will be "dried up" by hunger: their energy, their vitality is exhausted under the weight of divine punishment.
2. Beyond the physical sense, "to dry up" describes a state of total withering, a progressive destruction. The word paints the agony of one who, little by little, loses all that animates them.
3. It is also a form of annihilation: to be dried up is to be reduced to nothing, consumed, completely destroyed—the final state of divine judgment on unfaithfulness.
H4198.origine: The Hebrew word מָזֶה belongs to the family that expresses exhaustion and deprivation. Its root evokes the idea of emptying, depriving of substance. The underlying image is that of drying up: what was full becomes hollow, what was alive becomes inert. Related terms in the Hebrew Bible all designate states of lack, extinction, or absence.
H4198.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 32:24, in the context of the Song of Moses. Moses enumerates the curses that God will send upon the unfaithful people: hunger, fever, diseases, and attacks from wild beasts will "dry them up." It is a rare and necessarily dramatic term, chosen to express total and methodical annihilation—the judgment of God against apostasy.
H4198.portee: This word reminds us that unfaithfulness and rejection of the covenant lead to exhaustion and spiritual death. For the believer, it illustrates the ruin caused by distancing from God. But it also calls for faithfulness: only obedience preserves life and vitality in the relationship with the Lord.

sens: Son of Reuel and grandson of Esau
Edomite chief during the time of the patriarchs
H4199.detail: 1. Mizza was one of the four sons of Reuel, who was himself the son of Esau and Basemath. He appears in the genealogy of the Edomites, the people descended from Esau, the twin brother of Jacob (Genesis 36:13). His name means "fear" in Hebrew, possibly reflecting the relationship that Esau or his descendants had with the Lord. 2. Mizza became the chief of an Edomite clan, as indicated by the phrase "chief Mizza" in the list of Edomite chiefs (Genesis 36:17). Although not detailed, this role shows that he was an important figure among the descendants of Esau during the patriarchal era.
H4199.origine: The name Mizza means "fear" or "dread" in Hebrew, derived from a root expressing fear or trembling. This name is part of the genealogy of Esau and his descendants, which the Bible preserves to show how the neighboring peoples of Israel were formed.
H4199.emploi: Mizza appears only three times in the Bible, all occurrences found in genealogies: twice in Genesis 36 (verses 13 and 17) where the Edomite chiefs are listed, and once in 1 Chronicles 1:37 where the genealogy of Esau is recounted. These three occurrences are part of the genealogical lists that connect the neighboring peoples of Israel to Esau and establish the identity of the people of Edom. Mizza is always mentioned alongside his three brothers: Nahath, Zerah, and Shammah.

sens: Action of going outside, leaving a place
Word or decree that is expressed, that becomes effective
Source of water, from which water springs
Place or moment of departure
Provenance, origin of something
Direction of the east, where the sun rises
H4161.detail:
1. The action of exiting or departing: a movement that goes outward, forward. In Ezekiel 12:4, the exiles prepare by taking their belongings "as exiles depart," the expression designating the gestures of departure.
2. A word or command that comes from the mouth and becomes reality or obligation: what is stated produces an effect. In Numbers 30:13, a vow "that comes from his lips" binds the one who pronounced it.
3. A source, a point from which water springs, either naturally or in response to the power of God. In Psalms 107:35, God turns the dry land into "springs of water."
4. The place or moment from which one departs, the exit itself. In 2 Chronicles 32:30, it refers to the "upper outlet" of the waters, that is, the point from which the water flows or escapes.
5. What comes from a place or source, the "issue" or production. Horses and wood "from" Egypt (1 Kings 10:28) are what is brought from Egypt.
6. The east, the direction from which the sun rises and goes. The word "east" in Psalms 65:9 takes up this image of the movement of the celestial body from its starting point.
H4161.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to go, to exit" (יצא). Literally, "motzaï" is a noun designating the action or place of this exit, this movement outward. This root is very common in biblical Hebrew and gives rise to words of the same family: the verb "to go out," the participle "the one who goes out," and all sorts of nouns constructed on this idea of movement outward. The fundamental image is that of crossing a boundary, moving from the inside to the outside, or remaining inside and expressing outwardly.
H4161.emploi: The word appears 26 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms, historical and prophetic books. It designates sometimes a physical movement (the exit from a place, the departure of an exile), sometimes a natural or divine process (water springing from a source, the sun rising), sometimes a word or decree that is realized (a vow that binds, a promise that is fulfilled). In Numbers 30:13 and 33:2, the word applies to what "comes out" of the mouth: the vow or the spoken word. In 2 Kings 2:21 and Isaiah 41:18, it is the water that "comes out" or springs from a healed source. In Ezekiel 42:11 and 43:11, it designates the "issue" or exit door of a building. The context always shows a movement or emanation: something that comes from somewhere and goes outward.
H4161.portee: This word reminds us that the word of God is never inert: it "comes out" of His mouth and is fulfilled (Isaiah 55:11). It also invites us to see how God brings forth life and blessing from sources that seem exhausted (Psalms 107:35, Isaiah 41:18). For the Christian, this term illustrates the creative and transformative power of God: what He says is, and what comes forth from Him bears the mark of His authority.
